entry.title: One-minute frequency disturbances from synchronization in power systems
entry.content:
Abstract

Electric power systems are evolving into cyber–physical infrastructures shaped by power electronics and digital control. As inverter-based generation alters system dynamics and digitalization heightens vulnerability to errors and attacks, cyber–physical coupling can also introduce subtle system-level effects. Here we show that grid-frequency time series worldwide exhibit a persistent 1-min oscillatory pattern whose origin has remained unexplained. We show that clock-synchronized control software in digitally controlled energy devices, particularly uninterruptible power supplies and battery energy storage systems, generates periodic power-demand peaks that propagate across voltage levels and can give rise to the observed pattern. The pattern amplitude has increased substantially in several grids over recent years, contributing to wear and tear in hydropower systems and motivating stricter frequency-control requirements. The rapid expansion of battery storage, data centres and the Internet-of-Things may further amplify such cyber–physical power oscillations, highlighting the need for improved control design.

The transition to a sustainable energy system requires advanced control methods to deal with increasing complexity and uncertainty1,2. As variable renewable energy sources such as wind and solar replace conventional generation, maintaining power balance requires accurate forecasting and real-time control of storage, backup generation and flexible demand3. At the same time, the electrification of sectors such as transport and heating is introducing millions of digitally controlled devices—electric vehicle chargers4, heat pumps5 and smart appliances6—into the grid. Furthermore, data centres add additional software-dependent loads7. Together, these trends are reshaping the power system into a cyber–physical infrastructure, where physical devices and digital control are deeply intertwined. In this new paradigm, system reliability increasingly depends not only on the physical properties of generation and load but also on the design, timing and coordination of software-controlled devices across all layers of operation8.

While cyber–physical integration enables unprecedented levels of efficiency and flexibility, it also introduces new systemic risks9. Historical events underscore the stakes: inadequate situational awareness contributed to the 2003 North American blackout10, and software-driven control failures have played critical roles in recent major outages11,12. Beyond failures and malicious attacks, however, even benign control routines can become systemically relevant when many devices act coherently. Unintended synchronization can generate recurrent and potentially amplified oscillatory behaviour in large-scale cyber–physical energy systems.

Modern power systems exhibit oscillations across a broad range of time scales. Oscillations with characteristic periods around 1 min have previously been discussed as ultralow-frequency oscillations (ULFOs) and linked to resonance phenomena in hydropower turbine-governor systems13,14,15,16. However, resonance phenomena in classical control systems differ fundamentally from cyber–physical synchronization effects. Oscillations without external timing signals do not naturally explain patterns that remain phase-coherent over long time scales or occur reproducibly across diverse power systems.

In this Article, we identify and explain a coherent 1-min oscillation in power systems worldwide caused by cyber–physical synchronization effects. We show that the grid frequency, and thus the power balance, exhibits a highly regular periodic pattern with a period of exactly 1 min. Searching for potential causes of this pattern, we provide empirical evidence that clock-synchronized control actions in battery-based uninterruptible power supplies (UPSs) generate periodic power-demand peaks, and we demonstrate that this signal propagates across multiple voltage levels up to the transmission interface. More broadly, our results point to a class of cyber–physical power oscillations driven by externally synchronized control software.

The identified synchronization mechanism is not specific to UPSs or battery systems, but reflects a general property of digitally controlled devices operating with external timing signals or periodic software routines. The rapid expansion of battery storage, data-centre infrastructure and Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices increases the relevance of cyber–physical risks in power-system operation. At the same time, decreasing system inertia makes power systems more sensitive to coherent power imbalances17. Indeed, we observe that the amplitude of the 1-min pattern has increased in several grids. The oscillation contributes to wear and tear, especially in hydropower turbines18, and has motivated stricter load–frequency control requirements19. Our results indicate that coherent cyber–physical oscillations can be mitigated directly at their source through improved control design.

A universal 1-min pattern in the grid frequency

The grid frequency is a key observable in power-system operation, reflecting the balance between generation and load: it rises when generation exceeds demand and falls when demand outpaces supply. Maintaining the nominal frequency of 50 Hz or 60 Hz therefore requires continuous balancing by load–frequency control systems20.

Large frequency deviations occur during contingencies and severe disturbances and can endanger system stability21,22. Smaller but recurrent deviations arise continuously during normal operation through both stochastic fluctuations and deterministic mechanisms23,24.

To identify dominant recurrent patterns, we carry out a Fourier analysis of grid-frequency time series f(t) from multiple power systems worldwide (Fig. 1). The investigated grids span five continents and range in size from approximately 400,000 customers in Iceland to more than 400 million customers in the Continental European synchronous area.

Recurrent frequency deviations occur across a broad range of time scales. Figure 2 summarizes the dominant Fourier peaks and characteristic patterns observed in the Continental European grid.

At slow time scales, pronounced peaks occur at periods of 15 min and 60 min together with their higher harmonics. These deterministic frequency deviations (DFDs) arise from electricity trading, where generation is adjusted approximately stepwise at the boundaries of market intervals while electrical demand evolves continuously25,26,27,28. This phenomenon is not unique to the Continental European grid; it also appears in other markets such as Scandinavia (cf. Supplementary Fig. 1).

Additional recurrent patterns occur at shorter time scales, including oscillations due to load variations in data centres29, inter-area oscillations between geographically separated groups of synchronous generators30 and persistent forced oscillations of previously unresolved origin31 with periods of one to a few seconds. At even faster time scales, recent studies have identified sustained oscillations related to interactions of grid dynamics and data centres32 as well as subsynchronous oscillations in inverter-dominated grids33.

Against this background, we observe a remarkably narrow spectral peak at exactly 1 min in all investigated grids (Fig. 1). The signal is particularly pronounced in large interconnected systems in Europe, North America and Australia, but remains clearly visible in smaller grids such as Malaysia, South Korea and South Africa, as well as in island systems such as Mallorca, Ireland and Iceland. Its extremely narrow spectrum indicates a precisely timed and phase-coherent process that remains stable over multiple years. Related oscillations with characteristic periods around 1 min have previously been described as ULFOs13. In addition, we observe a weaker peak around 100 s whose origin remains uncertain. What causes this universal 1-min pattern?

Characterization of the 1-min pattern

To characterize the universal 1-min pattern, we divide the frequency time series f(t) into chunks of length τ. For every chunk, we compute a characteristic minutely profile s(t), referred to as the waveform in the following. More precisely, s(t) is the average over all minutes in the respective chunk for a given second of the minute t (see the Methods for details). Typically, we use chunks of length τ = 1 h to remove the hourly patterns induced by market effects, indicated by the subscript h. Furthermore, we define the hourly amplitude as

to characterize the strength of the pattern.

Figure 3a–c summarizes the waveform properties for the Continental European grid. The amplitude exhibits a pronounced daily modulation, with weaker signals during the night and stronger amplitudes during daytime operation. By contrast, the waveform shape remains remarkably stable: the frequency is typically highest at the beginning of the minute and then decreases for a few seconds (night) up to half a minute (day). Comparable behaviour is observed across multiple grids (Supplementary Fig. 2), although the precise waveform shape differs between systems.

The waveform remains phase-coherent and stable over multiple years across all investigated grids. Such long-term coherence is difficult to reconcile with intrinsic oscillatory modes of the power system and instead points to drivers synchronized to a stable external clock.

These observations indicate a recurrent pattern in the underlying power imbalance. In general, the rate of change of frequency follows the instantaneous power imbalance in the grid. The relation between both quantities can be described by the aggregated swing equation34,35,

where ΔP(t) denotes the power imbalance, D is a damping coefficient, fref the reference frequency and Erot denotes the total rotational energy of online synchronous machines, which quantifies the system inertia. Accordingly, the observed decrease in frequency implies that demand exceeds generation during the first half of each minute.

Load–frequency control can amplify disturbances at specific frequencies via feedback effects in the power imbalance ΔP(t). Hydropower turbine-governor systems have therefore been suggested as a possible origin of oscillations with periods around 1 min (refs. 15,16). Recent work has furthermore linked 1-min oscillations to periodic set-point updates in secondary frequency control36. We likewise observe a 1-min pattern in the secondary control set-point in German control areas (Supplementary Fig. 3 and Supplementary Note 1).

To assess the role of hydropower dynamics, we perform complementary mechanistic and data-driven analyses (Supplementary Notes 2 and 3). A mechanistic model of hydropower plant control in the Scandinavian grid reveals an internal resonance that can produce oscillatory responses with characteristic periods around 1 min (Supplementary Figs. 4–9). In parallel, an explainable machine learning analysis identifies systematic correlations between hydropower commitment and the signal amplitude in the Continental European grid (Supplementary Fig. 10). However, neither analysis supports the interpretation that hydropower dynamics alone can explain the long-term phase coherence and cross-system reproducibility of the observed signal. Instead, the results indicate that hydropower can amplify externally driven coherent disturbances or generate transient incoherent oscillations with periods close to 1 min.

The characteristic shape of the 1-min pattern is remarkably stable, while its amplitude changes over time. Figure 3d shows the long-term evolution for three European grids where sufficient historical data are available. We observe that the amplitude increased substantially in the British and Scandinavian grids after 2015, reaching peak values in 2020.

One important factor contributing to the observed increase is the reduction of effective system inertia during the transition from synchronous generation to converter-interfaced renewable power sources17. According to equation (2), lower inertia increases the frequency response to a given coherent power imbalance. A temporary increase during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) lockdown in 2020 further suggests that changes in system conditions, including effective system inertia and demand composition, can enhance the signal amplitude (Supplementary Fig. 11 and Supplementary Note 4).

In the Scandinavian grid, amplitudes regularly exceeded 10 mHz, raising concerns among grid operators and utilities because oscillatory operation contributes to wear and tear of hydropower turbines providing primary control18. As a consequence, Scandinavian transmission system operators revised the requirements for frequency containment reserves in 202319. The revised prequalification procedures include sine-wave tests in the range of 10–300 s together with stricter damping and activation requirements intended to suppress oscillatory responses (cf. Supplementary Note 5). Following these revisions, amplitudes above 10 mHz were no longer observed in 2025 (Fig. 3d). These developments demonstrate that the recurrent 1-min oscillation already has operational relevance, even though current mitigation strategies primarily address amplification rather than the underlying source.

Identifying the drivers of the 1-min pattern

Frequency deviations reflect imbalances between generation and load as described by equation (2). For the Continental European synchronous area, the overall network power-frequency characteristic is estimated as K = 26.68 GW Hz−1 (ref. 20). Accordingly, a periodic frequency variation with an amplitude of 3 mHz corresponds to a coherent power variation of approximately 80 MW. Which devices generate this signal?

A comparison of measurements from the transmission and distribution levels in the Continental European grid shows that the waveform at the distribution level is slightly phase-advanced (Supplementary Figs. 12–14 and Supplementary Note 6). This suggests that the driving sources are located in the distribution system, while large synchronous generators respond to the resulting imbalance. We therefore investigate high-resolution measurements from local distribution networks.

Forschungszentrum Jülich operates a comprehensive measurement infrastructure in its campus distribution grid. We analyse high-resolution active-power measurements from multiple buildings and transformers to identify potential drivers of the signal (cf. Supplementary Fig. 15 and Supplementary Note 7).

A clear 1-min component is observed only at a subset of measurement locations. In total, four buildings exhibit a pronounced periodic signal in the bus-level active-power measurements (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Figs. 16–17). Importantly, all affected buildings contain battery-based UPSs, whereas none of the measured buildings without UPS installations show such a pattern.

These observations identify battery energy management systems (EMSs), particularly in UPS applications, as prime drivers of the 1-min signal. Their control algorithms can induce periodic power-demand peaks at fixed 1-min intervals that propagate through the grid and contribute to coherent frequency variations. More generally, the results point to a broader class of cyber–physical synchronization effects arising from digitally controlled devices operating on externally synchronized clocks or periodic software routines.

To investigate this mechanism in detail, we analyse a UPS installation in Building 3 on the Jülich campus (Supplementary Table 1). Measurements include (1) the DC battery current, (2) AC currents and power flows upstream and downstream of the UPS and (3) transformer-level power flows up to the connection with the public 110-kV high-voltage grid (Fig. 5a).

On the DC side of the UPS, at the battery terminals, narrow current peaks recurring every 1 min are observed (Fig. 5b). The origin of these current peaks was independently confirmed by the manufacturer to be periodic self-tests executed by the battery EMS, confirming our interpretation. Similar minute-scale diagnostic routines are also documented for other commercial UPS systems (cf. Supplementary Note 8). On the AC side, after subtracting the demand of the building connected downstream of the UPS, these 1-min peaks are not clearly visible in the three-phase current time series. However, Fourier analysis reveals a persistent 1-min component in the currents (Fig. 5c). The corresponding periodic power demand can be traced across several transformers and a bus bar, up to the transformer connecting to the public 110-kV grid (Fig. 5d). These findings demonstrate that the pattern originating on the DC side propagates into the high-voltage grid.

We next investigate the temporal stability of the signal and the role of clock synchronization. Figure 6a compares weekly waveforms sw(t) for three transformers supplying buildings equipped with UPS systems. The measurements reveal markedly different behaviours.

In Building 3, the waveform exhibits a slowly drifting sawtooth-like structure characterized by a sharp increase followed by a gradual decay. This behaviour is consistent with the response of the UPS and grid infrastructure to narrow periodic current peaks on the DC side, effectively acting as a low-pass filter.

By contrast, Buildings 1 and 4 show phase-stable waveforms with recurring power-demand peaks shortly after the beginning of each minute. Such coherent demand peaks naturally explain the emergence of the corresponding frequency pattern at grid level. Notably, the UPS systems in Buildings 1 and 4 originate from different manufacturers than the system installed in Building 3, emphasizing the importance of EMS implementation and control design.

Synchronization of digitally controlled devices is commonly achieved using the Network Time Protocol (NTP)37, which synchronizes local clocks to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). To assess the influence of clock synchronization on UPS operation, we performed comparative measurements for the Building 3 EMS with NTP synchronization disabled and enabled.

With NTP disabled, the UPS self-test signatures show a slow drift with respect to UTC. With NTP enabled, the daily progression of the UPS self-test signatures becomes substantially more pronounced, reaching approximately 6 s per day (Fig. 6b, Supplementary Fig. 18 and Supplementary Note 9). The progression is not continuous; instead, the phase remains stable during the day and is shifted at midnight. These observations indicate that periodic EMS routines operate on internally scheduled 1-min cycles whose timing is regularly reinitialized through external clock synchronization.

Future developments and mitigation

The observed 1-min signal is already substantial in several power systems, although it has not reached a safety critical level. Nevertheless, several ongoing developments in modern energy systems make a further increase plausible and suggest that mitigation strategies should be implemented before the effect becomes more severe.

One important trend is the rapid deployment of digitally controlled energy devices. Battery capacities are increasing strongly38,39 (Fig. 7a), while data centres equipped with large UPS installations account for a growing fraction of electricity demand7,40. In Ireland, where data centres reached approximately 18% of national electricity demand in 202241, the magnitude of the minute-scale frequency drop increased from approximately 3 mHz to 12 mHz between 2016 and 2021 (Fig. 7b). More recent measurements show that individual frequency drops can exceed 20 mHz and, when superimposed on larger frequency excursions, can bring the system close to the limits of the target operating range (Supplementary Figs. 19–21 and Supplementary Note 10).

In parallel, the proliferation of IoT devices42 introduces additional loads operating with externally synchronized clocks or periodic software routines. We observe corresponding periodic power signatures both in a smart baking oven and in Raspberry-Pi clusters (Fig. 7c, Supplementary Figs. 22 and 23 and Supplementary Note 11).

A second important trend is the reduction of system inertia during the transition from fossil-fuelled synchronous generation to converter-interfaced renewable generation. Lower inertia increases the frequency response to a given coherent power imbalance17 and has been linked to stronger ULFOs14. This effect is illustrated by the Mallorca grid, where the withdrawal of a major coal-fired power plant from regular operation at the end of 2019 coincided with an increase of the 1-min amplitude by approximately 50% (Fig. 7d, Supplementary Fig. 24 and Supplementary Note 12). This increase is consistent with a reduction in effective inertia, although concurrent changes in frequency-control operation may also have contributed.

These examples indicate that the 1-min signal can grow through both sides of the frequency response: coherent power variations may increase as clocked devices proliferate, while the same power variations lead to larger frequency deviations as inertia decreases. This does not imply an imminent stability threat, but it makes the phenomenon relevant for future system operation, especially because deterministic deviations can add to stochastic fluctuations and other recurrent patterns (Supplementary Figs. 25–30 and Supplementary Note 13).

Several mitigation routes are available. System-level measures can reduce the frequency impact of deterministic disturbances. In particular, revisions of frequency-control regulations in the Scandinavian19 and Australian43 grids substantially reduced the amplitude of the observed signal (Fig. 7e). However, such measures primarily mitigate the frequency response rather than the underlying coherent power modulation.

The root cause of cyber–physical power oscillations can be addressed directly through control design. Clocked internal routines should avoid simultaneous power adjustments across many devices, for example, by using randomized scheduling, adaptive offsets or event-driven rather than strictly time-driven execution. This approach is technically feasible for utility-scale batteries and UPS systems, where software updates can be deployed centrally. Indeed, following our communication with the manufacturer, a software update was issued that removed the strict periodicity of the current peaks in one battery block of the investigated UPS system (Fig. 7f). However, self-tests still occur at discrete times such that the root cause has been resolved only partially (Supplementary Fig. 31 and Supplementary Note 9).

Mitigation may be more challenging for household-scale IoT devices, where software updates and control standards are less coordinated than in utility-scale infrastructure. These observations highlight the importance of early coordination between manufacturers, system operators and regulators as digitally synchronized energy devices continue to proliferate.

Discussion

Cybersecurity and the management of power imbalances are widely recognized as central challenges for future power systems44,45. Maintaining a stable frequency becomes increasingly difficult as system inertia declines17,22, while cybersecurity is threatened by failures and malicious attacks9. Here, we highlight a more subtle systemic challenge arising from the cyber–physical coupling of modern power systems.

We show that the grid frequency in power systems across five continents exhibits a persistent and highly stable recurrence with a period of exactly 1 min. While aspects of such ULFOs have been reported previously36, the origin of their long-term coherence has remained unclear. We provide evidence that the observed signal is probably linked to unintended synchronization of digitally controlled devices whose control actions are scheduled by clocked software processes. When synchronized across many devices, such routines can generate coherent power variations at system scale. The growing relevance of this mechanism is illustrated by the Irish power system, where the initial frequency drop of the 1-min signal increased to 12 mHz in 2021, reaching substantially larger values during individual periods (Supplementary Fig. 20). This increase coincides with the rapid expansion of data centres equipped with large UPS installations, whose electricity demand reached approximately 18% of national consumption in 2022. The growing importance of data centres for power-system planning and operation has brought renewed attention to their dynamic interaction with the grid7,46, but the role of synchronized UPS control has largely been overlooked. Future work should develop detailed mechanistic models that capture the interaction between power-system operation and digitally controlled loads, including data centres and clock-synchronized devices.

More generally, many modern energy devices, including large-scale batteries, photovoltaic inverters and smart appliances, rely on embedded software and external time synchronization and may therefore contribute to coherent cyber–physical power oscillations. Beyond the highly coherent behaviour observed here, model-based studies suggest that even partial temporal coherence across large device populations may already produce measurable aggregate effects on the power balance47. The rapid projected expansion of battery storage systems and IoT devices is therefore likely to increase the relevance of such synchronization effects in future power systems. At the same time, decreasing system inertia increases the frequency response to coherent power imbalances17, while hydropower turbine-governor dynamics may further amplify coherent oscillations through resonant feedback effects.

Mitigation can proceed along two complementary routes. System-level measures, such as stricter primary frequency-control requirements, can reduce the frequency impact of deterministic disturbances, as observed in the Scandinavian and Australian grids. However, such measures mainly suppress the response to coherent power modulation rather than its origin. Addressing the root cause requires improved control design, for example through randomized scheduling, adaptive offsets or event-driven instead of strictly time-driven routines. Our measurements demonstrate that such mitigation is technically feasible, although coordinated implementation across heterogeneous large-scale device populations remains challenging.

Our results highlight the increasingly important role of software and digital control in modern energy systems. Traditionally, power-system stability has primarily been analysed in terms of physical infrastructure and control dynamics. Increasing digitalization, however, requires an integrated perspective in which control logic, software timing and synchronization are treated as integral components of power-system stability. More broadly, our findings demonstrate that collective effects are central to future cyber–physical power systems and can emerge both through interactions in the physical grid and through digital interconnections.

Methods Data sources and processing

To monitor grid behaviour, load profiles and power flows on the Jülich research campus, over 80 PQI-DA smart power quality (PQ) meters by a-eberle have been deployed48. These devices comply with the following PQ standards: EN 50160, IEEE 519, IEC 61000-2-2, IEC 61000-4-30, IEC 61000-2-12, IEC 61000-4-7, IEC 61000-2-4 and IEC 61000-4-15, as well as NRS 048. In particular, they are Class A devices that comply with the IEC 61000-4-30 Ed. 3 (2015) standards49, ensuring highly accurate measurements of frequency, voltage and current at the fundamental frequency, as well as other PQ phenomena. Communication with the meters relies on the Modbus Transmission Control Protocol, which provides data via standardized registers for various aggregation intervals, from 200 ms up to 2 h, as defined in the IEC standards50,51. During normal operation, key electrical quantities such as frequency, voltage, current and power are stored on the FIWARE-based Campus Information and Communications Technology platform52. We use data with 3-s resolution. Additional details are provided in Supplementary Note 7.

Frequency data with a resolution of 1 s on transmission grid-level for the Continental European, British and Scandinavian grids are provided by the transmission system operators53,54,55. The data have been pre-processed using the scripts provided in ref. 56. We use data from 1 January 2015 until 31 December 2025. For Australia, frequency data is available with 4-s resolution from the transmission system operator57. In addition, we obtained frequency data from Ireland for 2016 with 1-s resolution directly from the network operator EirGrid. Low-resolution frequency data in Ireland for 1 month in 2026 has been scraped directly from EirGrid’s Smart Grid Dashboard58.

Frequency data for USA, Malaysia, South Korea, South Africa, Mallorca, Ireland (2021) and Iceland are measured on the distribution grid-level using the Electrical Data Recorder described in refs. 59,60; details are provided in Supplementary Note 14. The Electrical Data Recorder measures voltage and current waveforms at high temporal resolution and derives the fundamental system frequency using a filtered zero-crossing method61. This approach is well suited for capturing frequency variations on time scales of seconds and above, as considered in this study, whereas the analysis of faster dynamics or strongly modulated signals may require alternative frequency definitions and demodulation methods62. These standalone measurements vary in length and cover approximately 5 years (Mallorca), 10 months (US West), 4 months (South Africa), 2.5 weeks (US East), 2.5 months (Iceland), 3.5 months (South Korea), 1 month (Ireland, 2021) and 1.5 weeks (Malaysia). A comparison of frequency data from the three different sources is provided in Supplementary Note 14 and Supplementary Fig. 32. The exact measurement periods are provided in Supplementary Figs. 33–35.

Frequency data from Belfort, Málaga and Porto for illustrating the inter-area oscillations over a period of 20 s, with a time resolution of 0.1 s in Fig. 2d, is provided by the Gridradar initiative63. The remaining data from Karlsruhe, Elk and Kaunas in Fig. 2d are also measured by Electrical Data Recorder devices.

The data on electricity generation from the coal-fired power plant in Mallorca are taken from ref. 64. In our analysis, the 5-min resolution dataset is aggregated into daily averages.

If not explicitly stated otherwise, we use UTC to index the time series in order to avoid ambiguity due to daylight saving time. As we analyse the hourly amplitudes, we further remove full hours of time series data if a single data point is missing or corrupted. The missing data after pre-processing is summarized in Supplementary Figs. 33–35.

Waveform and amplitude

Let f(t) be a discrete time series for some time interval t ∈ [t0, t1] of length τ = t1 − t0 with sampling time Δt. In particular, we consider the grid frequency and the real power load. We compute the average waveform s(t) of a recurrent temporal pattern with period T by averaging over blocks of length T. That is, we divide the interval [t0, t1] into \(N=\frac{{t}_{1}-{t}_{0}}{T}\) blocks of length T and average f(t) over these blocks.

for t ∈ [0, T). From the waveform, we define the amplitude \({a}_{[{t}_{0},{t}_{1}],T}\) of the pattern over the interval [t0, t1] as

To quantify how waveforms and amplitudes evolve over time, we divide the entire measurement period into non-overlapping 1-h segments and evaluate the waveform and its amplitude separately for each segment. Specifically, for each hour h we set t0 = h and t1 = h + 1 h, and denote the resulting waveform as sh,T(t) and the corresponding amplitude as ah,T. For simplicity, we drop the subscript \(T=1\,\min\) in the main text.

Similarly, we define daily sd,T(t), weekly sw,T(t) and monthly sm,T(t) waveforms and amplitudes by setting τ to 1 day, 1 week and 1 month, respectively, and averaging over the corresponding number of blocks N.

The datasets generated and analysed in this study that are not available from existing public sources are available via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17366692 (ref. 65), with two exceptions arising from third-party ownership. entry.title: The She-Wolves of Jülich
HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
entry.content:
HackerTube

It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org!

Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews, filtered them, ran Sonnet over them in a Workflow (Claude Code feature), got rid of spam, and narrowed everything down to 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila!

HackerTube:

Contains quality content Uses the 50% thumbnail instead of the uploaded thumbnail Custom and good ForYou recommendations without any user accounts, storing state in local browser session Keyboard shortcuts Export of the site's data available to give to your agent to easily create your own version

This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5 <3.

EDIT: A little bit more on my process. I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac). I use Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I don't actually do anything resembling traditional engineering anymore (read/write code, run commands in a terminal, or etc.), I only talk to Claude and have it do everything. In this case, the only "manual work" I did was: 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box and 3) I bought the domain name. I worked on this in between Claude's actual work so it still feels a little bit like team work :) Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, deploy, secure, harden and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

entry.title: Bidirectional charging during grid outages
entry.content:
Bidirectional Charging During Grid Outages September 7th, 2026 preparedness, solar, tech

The basic problem is that while several manufacturers support having the car power your house when the grid is down ("V2H"), they generally treat it as a separate discharging-only mode. For example, the GM V2H Bundle documentation says "During a power outage, the GM Energy Home Hub safely disconnects your home from the local power grid and enables backup power to flow from the GM Energy Inverter throughout your home" and "Once power is restored, your GM EV will automatically end the discharge session and begin charging" without any mention of recharging the car when the grid is down.

For Fords, automatically powering your house during a grid outage was a big selling point in the F150 Lightning marketing campaign, but they now say "The Ford Charge Station Pro, required for Automatic Home Backup Power, is no longer for sale", probably because the F150 Lightning has been discontinued. And it looks to me like even then they didn't support bidirectional charging during a grid outage. The only option today is V2H via a transfer switch, which doesn't let you charge an F150.

For Kia, there's Wallbox's Quasar 2. Unfortunately this is a mess where Wallbox is very enthusiastic and says V2H works, but then customers run into trouble actually trying to use it. And it doesn't work with current models, plus "Solar Charging cannot be used simultaneously with ... V2H".

The only way I can see to do this today is with Tesla Powershare + Cybertruck, which says "If the system includes a UL 1741-listed solar system and there is capacity in the backup panel, ensure the solar system is included in the backup circuit to allow Cybertruck to recharge during an outage." But I don't want a Cybertruck, and (counting the cost of a Cybertruck over a vehicle we'd normally buy) this would be way more expensive than the Enphase 10C I'm considering installing.

Another possibility is that Enphase is planning on shipping a bidirectional EV charger, but I don't see anything more recent than a 2026-02-02 announcement that they're "targeting volume production beginning in Q4 2026" and they say "projected vehicle compatibility and bidirectional functionality will depend on automaker enablement, vehicle software, applicable standards, and final product specifications." I suspect it will slip into 2027, MA availability will be even later, and when it does come out I'd need to buy a specific new EV (expensive).

I don't want to wait that long to get good backup power in place, since I want to be prepared for a world that might change quickly in the next few years. So I'll probably go ahead with the smaller emergencies-only battery.

[1] All of this assumes we have an electric car. Which we don't, but our shared Honda Fit is a 2013 and while it's been a fantastic car I don't expect it to last that much longer. A plug-in hybrid or full EV are possibilities for a next car. I think our families are unusually poorly suited for full EVs since we don't use the car much (minimal gas savings and pollution reduction) and a larger than typical proportion of our trips are long (ex: driving to play a dance).

entry.title: A Chemical Hunger (2021)
entry.content:
The study of obesity is the study of mysteries.

Mystery 1: The Obesity Epidemic

The first mystery is the obesity epidemic itself. It’s hard for a modern person to appreciate just how thin we all were for most of human history. A century ago, the average man in the US weighed around 155 lbs. Today, he weighs about 195 lbs. About 1% of the population was obese back then. Now it’s about 36%.

Back in the 1890s, the federal government had a board of surgeons examine several thousand Union Army veterans who fought in the Civil War. This was several decades after the end of the war, so by this point the veterans were all in their 40’s or older. This gives us a snapshot of what middle-aged white men looked like in the 1890s. When we look at their data, we find that they had an average BMI of about 23 (overweight is a BMI of 25 and obese is a BMI of 30 or more). Only about 3% of them were obese. In comparison, middle-aged white men in the year 2000 had an average BMI of around 28. About 24% were obese in early middle age, increasing to 41% by the time the men were in their 60s.

(Most experts consider measures like body fat percentage to be better measures of adiposity than BMI, and we agree. Unfortunately, nearly every source reports BMI, and most don’t report body fat percentage. Here, we use BMI so that we can compare different sources to one another.)

It’s not just that we’re a little fatter than our great-grandparents — the entire picture is different.

People in the 1800s did have diets that were very different from ours. But by conventional wisdom, their diets were worse, not better. They ate more bread and almost four times more butter than we do today. They also consumed more cream, milk, and lard. This seems closely related to observations like the French Paradox — the French eat a lot of fatty cheese and butter, so why aren’t they fatter and sicker?

Our great-grandparents (and the French) were able to maintain these weights eﬀortlessly. They weren’t all on weird starvation diets or crazy fasting routines. And while they probably exercised more on average than we do, the minor diﬀerence in exercise isn’t enough to explain the enormous diﬀerence in weight. Many of them were farmers or laborers, of course, but plenty of people in 1900 had cushy desk jobs, and those people weren’t obese either.

Something seems to have changed. But surprisingly, we don’t seem to have any idea what that thing was.

Mystery 2: An Abrupt Shift

Another thing that many people are not aware of is just how abrupt this change was. Between 1890 and 1976, people got a little heavier. The average BMI went from about 23 to about 26. This corresponds with rates of obesity going from about 3% to about 10%. The rate of obesity in most developed countries was steady at around 10% until 1980, when it suddenly began to rise.

Today the rate of obesity in Italy, France, and Sweden is around 20%. In 1975, there was no country in the world that had an obesity rate higher than 15%.

This wasn’t a steady, gentle trend as food got better, or diets got worse. People had access to plenty of delicious, high-calorie foods back in 1965. Doritos were invented in 1966, Twinkies in 1930, Oreos in 1912, and Coca-Cola all the way back in 1886. So what changed in 1980?

Common wisdom today tells us that we get heavier as we get older. But historically, this wasn’t true. In the past, most people got slightly leaner as they got older. Those Civil War veterans we mentioned above had an average BMI of 23.2 in their 40s and 22.9 in their 60’s. In their 40’s, 3.7% were obese, compared to 2.9% in their 60s. We see the same pattern in data from 1976-1980: people in their 60s had slightly lower BMIs and were slightly less likely to be obese than people in their 40s (See the table below). It isn’t until the 1980s that we start to see this trend reverse. Something fundamental about the nature of obesity has changed.

Mystery 3: The Ongoing Crisis

Things don’t seem to be getting any better. A couple decades ago, rising obesity rates were a frequent topic of discussion, debate, and concern. But recently it has received much less attention; from the lack of press and popular coverage, you might reasonably assume that if we aren’t winning the fight against obesity, we’ve gotten at least to a stalemate.

But this simply isn’t the case. Americans have actually gotten more obese over the last decade. In fact, obesity increased more than twice as much between 2010 and 2018 than it did between 2000 and 2008.

Rates of obesity are also increasing worldwide. As The Lancet notes, “unlike other major causes of preventable death and disability, such as tobacco use, injuries, and infectious diseases, there are no exemplar populations in which the obesity epidemic has been reversed by public health measures.”

All of this is, to say the least, very mysterious.

1.1 Weird Mysteries

Then there are the weird mysteries.

Mystery 4: Hunter-Gatherers

A common assumption is that humans evolved eating a highly varied diet of wild plants and animals, that our bodies still crave variety, and that we would be better off with a more varied diet. But when we look at modern hunter-gatherers, we see this isn’t true. The !Kung San of Tanzania get about 40% of their calories from a single food source, the mongongo nut, with another 40% coming from meat. But the !Kung are extremely lean (about 110lbs on average) and have excellent cardiovascular health.

Of course, variety isn’t everything. You would also expect that people need to eat the right diet. A balanced diet, with the right mix of macronutrients. But again, this doesn’t seem to be the case. Hunter-gatherer societies around the world have incredibly different diets, some of them very extreme, and almost never suffer from obesity.

Historically, different cultures had wildly different diets — some hunter-gatherers ate diets very high in sugar, some very high in fat, some very high in starch, etc. Some had diets that were extremely varied, while others survived largely off of just two or three foods. Yet all of these different groups remained lean. This is strong evidence against the idea that a high-fat, high-sugar, high-starch, low-variety, high-variety, etc. diet could cause obesity.

A Tanzanian hunter-gatherer society called the Hadza get about 15 percent of their calories from honey. Combined with all the sugar they get from eating fruit, they end up eating about the same amount of sugar as Americans do. Despite this, the Hadza do not exhibit obesity. Another group, the Mbuti of the Congo, eat almost nothing but honey during the rainy season, when honey can provide up to 80% of the calories in their diet. These are all unrefined sugars, of course, but the Kuna of Panama, though mostly hunter-gatherers, also obtain white sugar and some sugar-containing foods from trade. Their diet is 65% carbohydrate and 17% sugar, which is more sugar than the average American currently consumes. Despite this the Kuna are lean, with average BMIs around 22-23.

The Inuit, by contrast, traditionally ate a diet consisting primarily of seal meat and blubber, with approximately 50% of their calories coming from fat. This diet is quite low in fruits and vegetables, but obesity was virtually unknown until the arrival of western culture. The Maasai are an even more extreme example, subsisting on a diet composed “almost exclusively of milk, blood, and meat”. They drink “an average of 3 to 5 quarts/day of their staple: milk supplemented with cow’s blood and meat“. This adds up to about 3000 calories per day, 66% of those calories being from fat. (They also sometimes eat honey and tree bark.) But the Maasai are also quite lean, with the average BMI for both men and women being again in the range of 22-23, increasing very slightly over age.

Kitava is a Melanesian island largely isolated from the outside world. In 1990, Staffan Lindeberg went to the island to study the diet, lifestyle, and health of its people. He found a diet based on starchy tubers and roots like yam, sweet potato, and taro, supplemented by fruit, vegetables, seafood, and coconut. Food was abundant and easy to come by, and the Kitavans ate as much as they wanted. “It is obvious from our investigations,” wrote Lindeberg, “that lack of food is an unknown concept, and that the surplus of fruits and vegetables regularly rots or is eaten by dogs.”

About 70% of the calories in the Kitavan diet came from carbohydrates. For comparison, the modern American diet is about 50% carbohydrates. Despite this, none of the Kitavans were obese. Instead they were in excellent health. Below, you’ll see a photo of a Kitavan man being examined by Lindeberg.

Kitavans didn’t even seem to gain weight in middle age. In fact, BMI was found to decrease with age. Many lived into their 80s or 90s, and Lindeberg even observed one man who he estimated to be 100 years old. None of the elderly Kitavans showed signs of dementia or memory loss. The Kitavans also had no incidence of diabetes, heart attacks, stroke, or cardiovascular disease, and were unfamiliar with the symptoms of these diseases. “The only cases of sudden death they could recall,” he reports, “were accidents such as drowning or falling from a coconut tree.”

Mystery 5: Lab Animals and Wild Animals

Humans aren’t the only ones who are growing more obese — lab animals and even wild animals are becoming more obese as well. Primates and rodents living in research colonies, feral rodents living in our cities, and domestic pets like dogs and cats are all steadily getting fatter and fatter. This can’t be attributed to changes in what they eat, because lab animals live in contained environments with highly controlled diets. They’re being fed the same foods as always, but for some reason, they’re getting fatter.

This seems to be true everywhere you look. Our pets may eat scraps from the table, but why would zoo animals, being fed by professionals, also be getting fatter? Even horses are becoming more obese. This is all very strange, and none of it fits with the normal explanations for the obesity epidemic.

Mystery 6: Palatable Human Food

Lab rats gain some weight on high-fat diets, but they gain much more weight on a “cafeteria diet” of human foods like Froot Loops [sic] and salami (see also here).

It used to be that if researchers needed obese rats for a study, they would just add fat to normal rodent chow. But it turns out that it takes a long time for rats to become obese on this diet. A breakthrough occurred one day when a graduate student happened to put a rat onto a bench where another student had left a half-finished bowl of Froot Loops. Rats are usually cautious around new foods, but in this case the rat wandered over and began scarfing down the brightly-colored cereal. The graduate student was inspired to try putting the rats on a diet of “palatable supermarket food”; not only Froot Loops, but foods like Doritos, pork rinds, and wedding cake. Today, researchers call these “cafeteria diets”.

Sure enough, on this diet the rats gained weight at unprecedented speed. All this despite the fact that the high-fat and cafeteria diets have similar nutritional profiles, including very similar fat/kcal percentages, around 45%. In both diets, rats were allowed to eat as much as they wanted. When you give a rat a high-fat diet, it eats the right amount and then stops eating, and maintains a healthy weight. But when you give a rat the cafeteria diet, it just keeps eating, and quickly becomes overweight. Something is making them eat more. “Palatable human food is the most effective way to cause a normal rat to spontaneously overeat and become obese,” says neuroscientist Stephan Guyenet in The Hungry Brain, “and its fattening effect cannot be attributed solely to its fat or sugar content.”

Rodents eating diets that are only high in fat or only high in carbohydrates don’t gain nearly as much weight as rodents eating the cafeteria diet. And this isn’t limited to lab rats. Raccoons and monkeys quickly grow fat on human food as well.

We see a similar pattern of results in humans. With access to lots of calorie-dense, tasty foods, people reliably overeat and rapidly gain weight. But again, it’s not just the contents. For some reason, eating more fat or sugar by itself isn’t as fattening as the cafeteria diet. Why is “palatable human food” so much worse for your waistline than its fat and sugar alone would suggest?

Mystery 7: Altitude

People who live at higher altitudes have lower rates of obesity. This is the case in the US, and also seems to be the case in other countries, for example Spain and Tibet. When US Army and Air Force service members are assigned to different geographic areas, they are more at risk of developing obesity in low-altitude areas than in high-altitude ones. Colorado is the highest-altitude US state and also has the lowest incidence of obesity.

If you look at a map of county-level obesity data in the United States, the Rockies, the Sierra Mountains, and the Appalachians stand out quite clearly:

Similarly, there is a condition called “altitude anorexia” where individuals who move to a high-altitude location sometimes lose a lot of weight all at once (see also here, here, and weight loss results here). This effect also seems to apply to lab rats who are moved to labs at higher altitudes.

In addition, there is some evidence for a similar relationship between altitude and the rate of diabetes, with people living at a higher elevation having lower rates of diabetes than those living near sea level, even when statistically adjusting for variables like age, BMI, and physical activity.

We know that oxygen and carbon dioxide vary with elevation, so you might expect that this is attributable to these differences. But the evidence is pretty thin. Combined with a low-calorie diet, exercise in a low-oxygen environment does seem to reduce weight more than exercise in normal atmospheric conditions, but not by much. Submarines have CO2 levels about 10 times higher than usual, but a US Navy study didn’t find evidence of consistent weight gain. The atmosphere itself can’t explain this.

One paper, Hypobaric Hypoxia Causes Body Weight Reduction in Obese Subjects from Lippl et al. (2012), claims to show a reduction in weight at high altitude and suggests that this weight loss is attributable to differences in oxygen levels. However, there are a number of problems with this paper and its conclusions. To begin with, there isn’t a control group, so this isn’t an experiment. Without an appropriate control, it’s hard to infer a causal relationship. What they actually show is that people brought to 2,650 meters lost a small amount of weight and had lower blood oxygen saturation, but this is unsurprising. Obviously if you bring people to 2,650 meters they will have lower blood oxygen, and there’s no evidence linking that to the reported weight loss. They don’t even report a correlation between blood oxygen saturation and weight loss, even though that would be the relevant test given the data they have. Presumably they don’t report it because it’s not significant. In addition there are major issues with multiple comparisons, which make their few significant findings hard to interpret (for more detail, see our full analysis of the paper).

Mystery 8: Diets Don’t Work

There’s a lot of disagreement about which diet is best for weight loss. People spend a lot of time arguing over how to diet, and about which diet is best. I’m sure people have come to blows over whether you lose more weight on keto or on the Mediterranean diet, but meta-analysis consistently finds that there is little difference between different diets.

Some people do lose weight on diets. Some of them even lose a lot of weight. But the best research finds that diets just don’t work very well in general, and that no one diet seems to be better than any other. For example, a 2013 review of 4 meta-analyses said:

Numerous randomized trials comparing diets differing in macronutrient compositions (eg, low-carbohydrate, low-fat, Mediterranean) have demonstrated differences in weight loss and metabolic risk factors that are small (ie, a mean difference of <1 kg) and inconsistent.

Most diets lead to weight loss of around 5-20 lbs, with minimal differences between them. Now, 20 lbs isn’t nothing, but it’s also not much compared to the overall size of the obesity epidemic. And even if someone does lose 20 lbs, in general they will gain most of it back within a year.

entry.title: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
entry.content:
The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks

One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users (DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this “frontend’s lost decade”, Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a pop culture, and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway).

For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the desire for greater DX. In other words, devs just liked the way it felt to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings. (Jonathan Haidt would likely agree with this assessment.)

But in the agentic era, when developers are no longer typing code by hand and are thus less constrained by DX, I still see vibes ruling the day (and not just in the sense of “vibe-coding”). Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc. Once again, these claims are often made without evidence. Whenever I read one of these accounts, I think to myself, “Where are the benchmarks?”

Well I got curious, so I wrote a benchmark. The structure of this benchmark is pretty straightforward:

Design a small but non-trivial Pokémon app using the PokéAPI (those who have followed my work will be unsurprised) Instruct agents to build the app with a particular JavaScript framework/meta-framework (e.g. Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, etc.) Test the output against a spec conformance suite (to avoid agent cheating) Evaluate the results in terms of development time, tokens spent, lines of code, and performance and accessibility scores in Lighthouse

The app is fairly simple: you’ve got a list of Pokémon with their types, moves, and data from various games. You can search, filter, etc.:

I should start off with some caveats: this is not a perfect experiment. This app represents only one holotype – it’s a relatively content-based site with little interactivity, closer to a Wikipedia than a Figma, GMail, etc. That said, I had to choose some app to build, and this one is at least easy to understand at a high level, and relatively straightforward to spec out and test.

To try to even the playing field, I had each framework/meta-framework use the official MCP or skills for that tool. I wanted to avoid accusations of “this framework is not well-represented in the training data, that’s why we built our MCP, we expect people to use it,” etc. I also didn’t over-specify the exact architecture to use (e.g. SSR vs CSR), nor did I specify that the app should be as performant as possible. I simply gave the spec to Opus 5.5 with high effort and told it to use the latest version of the given framework. Each agent ran in a sandbox and without any knowledge that it would be tested in Lighthouse on performance and accessibility, although it was given the conformance test suite.

Note I also didn’t mandate any CSS methodology, except to avoid using Tailwind, Bootstrap, or any other component framework, and to design based on a set of spec tokens to enforce some visual consistency. I didn’t want to make this test all about CSS, but instead about JS frameworks, CSR vs SSR, SPAs vs MPAs, etc. The resulting app is tested against a conformance suite based on the accessibility tree rather than the raw DOM to avoid mandating any particular HTML structure – one framework uses web components which rely on shadow DOM, so this was required.

One thing I learned from this experiment is that everything I’m measuring is very stochastic. LLMs are random-word generators, so sometimes you get a low dice-roll and an agent goes off on some weird tangent wasting a bunch of tokens, through no fault of the framework or its tools. Lighthouse itself can give inconsistent results as well: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) may decide that one image is the “largest” element, then pick another one on the next run. It’s hard to have a perfectly fair experiment, but running multiple iterations did help, and I’ve tried to be honest about the variance.

With all that throat-clearing out of the way, let’s get to the results.

Results

I’m going to break this down by multiple dimensions: cost to build, quality, and maintainability. For each framework/meta-framework, I took the median of 5 runs: in other words, I built the same app 5 times in the same framework. (Yes, this is the kind of zany thing you can do with coding agents these days.)

The exception was Angular, which failed to create a measurable app twice, so I took 3 iterations instead for some metrics. (This is explained below.)

Cost Cost per run, in US dollars Framework Hono+htmx $2.67 Astro $2.76 Nuxt $2.82 Vanilla $2.98 Next.js $3.14 Qwik $3.27 TanStack Start $3.54 SolidStart $3.79 React Router $3.81 SvelteKit $4.28 Gracile+Lit $4.65 Angular $4.97 02468

Note that this quotes the API prices directly from Claude Code and doesn’t actually represent how much money I spent. I’m on a Max plan, so this was just part of my overall $100/month.

Note also the variance: React Router’s median is roughly $1 worse than that of Hono+htmx, but the cheapest version of React Router ($2.82) is still cheaper than the most expensive version of Hono+htmx ($3.19). However some reliable patterns do emerge.

Most clearly, SvelteKit, Gracile+Lit, and Angular are more expensive to build than the other frameworks. For SvelteKit, this may be due to the fact that the agents read the SvelteKit v3 migration guide in every run, likely because it’s too new to be in Opus 5.5’s training data. Similarly for Gracile, the agents didn’t know the framework very well and either cloned the Gracile repo or read its compiled source from node_modules. For Angular it seems to be a function of the total code size (see below).

I should also mention that not every agent made use of an MCP/skill/Claude Code plugin, nor did every framework have one:

Click to see AI tool usage Framework Installed Used by the agents? Angular Angular MCP and Angular agent skills MCP in 3/5 runs, skill tool in 4/5 runs, skill files in 2/5 Astro Astro MCP server MCP in 2/5 runs Gracile+Lit N/A N/A Hono+htmx Hono skills Skill tool in 5/5 runs Next.js next-devtools-mcp and next-dev-loop skill Skill files in 1/5 runs, AGENTS.md in 2/5 runs Nuxt Nuxt MCP N/A Qwik N/A N/A React Router React Router skill Skill tool in 5/5 runs, skill files in 5/5 runs SolidStart N/A N/A SvelteKit Svelte Claude Code plugin MCP in 5/5 runs TanStack Start N/A Skill files in 2/5 runs Vanilla N/A N/A

For example, TanStack Start’s agent only discovered its skill files in 2/5 runs (they’re shipped in the node_modules of the project). For Nuxt, the MCP was never used by the agents. For Next.js, agents only read the skill file in 1/5 runs and the AGENTS.md in 2/5 runs. This is a wide range of results, which points back to the stochastic nature of LLMs. I still consider this a valid experiment, though, because I doubt many vibe-coders are shouting at their agents in all-caps to use the MCP (and plenty are probably skipping it entirely).

Also, if you’re wondering how I came up with Hono+htmx: essentially, I wanted htmx represented somehow, and Hono seemed like a fine pairing (i.e. as a JavaScript alternative to Rails/Django/etc.). As for Gracile+Lit, I wanted web components represented via their standard-bearer framework (Lit), and was only aware of Gracile as a meta-framework. If there are better candidates, then those would be great for a follow-up experiment.

For “Vanilla,” note that the agent was told to use “vanilla JavaScript or TypeScript with Vite, without a UI framework.” Surprisingly, this underperforms several frameworks, which seems to demonstrate that having some framework can be better than nothing (or better than raw Vite, anyway). Vite was chosen because it undergirds many frameworks and represents fairly standard and agnostic JavaScript infrastructure.

The total time and tokens track pretty closely with the cost:

Time per run Framework Astro 8.2 Hono+htmx 8.6 Nuxt 9.0 Vanilla 10.1 TanStack Start 10.3 Qwik 10.7 SvelteKit 10.8 Next.js 10.9 SolidStart 11.2 Gracile+Lit 12.1 React Router 12.5 Angular 17.2 0510152025
Tokens per run, in millions Framework Nuxt 3.85 Astro 4.13 Hono+htmx 4.26 Next.js 4.99 Vanilla 5.00 Qwik 5.64 TanStack Start 7.07 SolidStart 7.13 React Router 7.58 SvelteKit 8.53 Gracile+Lit 9.04 Angular 9.76 051015

The tokens, by the way, were reported by Claude Code. The duration is just the total wall-clock time.

Quality

Of course, because I think that outcomes matter, I also tested the agents with Lighthouse. As software developers, I think it’s important that we not only build things cheaply but also performantly and accessibly.

I should first note two caveats about my benchmark:

The Pokémon app is small and doesn’t represent a large, complex real-world application. Lighthouse and the Core Web Vitals in general are biased against SPAs, so the MPA frameworks are almost guaranteed to win on metrics like Total Blocking Time (TBT), JavaScript bytes, etc. I considered adding some in-app performance metrics but backed off because it added complexity and variability to the benchmark, and these would be metrics I invented as opposed to industry standards.

For simplicity’s sake, I’m only reporting the scores for the home page. There are other pages, but they all score fairly similarly or they have wild swings in metrics like LCP, so it just complicates things to include them.

In short: the Lighthouse scores for Performance, Accessibility, and CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) are nearly saturated and don’t vary much by framework:

Framework CLS Performance Accessibility Angular 0.000 98 100 Astro 0.000 100 100 Gracile+Lit 0.000 100 100 Hono+htmx 0.000 100 100 Next.js 0.000 99 100 Nuxt 0.000 100 100 Qwik 0.000 100 100 React Router 0.000 100 100 SolidStart 0.000 100 100 SvelteKit 0.000 100 100 TanStack Start 0.000 99 100 Vanilla 0.111 97 100

So to get some more interesting numbers, we need to look at other metrics. The most reliable one is the JavaScript bytes sent, which largely tracks the client-side framework size:

JavaScript bytes transferred Framework Astro 0 Vanilla 7 Gracile+Lit 8 Hono+htmx 18 SvelteKit 36 SolidStart 40 Qwik 40 Nuxt 84 Angular 93 React Router 115 TanStack Start 118 Next.js 142 050100150

The Total Blocking Time (TBT) is interesting in that it’s not purely a function of the JavaScript bytes; some of the apps spend more time on the main thread than others. That said, the numbers are all quite small:

Total Blocking Time (TBT) Framework Astro 0 Gracile+Lit 0 Hono+htmx 0 SvelteKit 0 Vanilla 0 TanStack Start 1 Qwik 3 SolidStart 11 React Router 17 Nuxt 40 Next.js 71 Angular 103 0255075100125

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) is highly variable due to the aforementioned issues with the metric itself. As expected, though, it does broadly punish SPAs and reward MPAs:

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) Framework Astro 810 Gracile+Lit 956 Hono+htmx 978 Qwik 979 SvelteKit 1130 SolidStart 1204 Vanilla 1667 Nuxt 1727 React Router 1729 Angular 1954 TanStack Start 2028 Next.js 2090 05001000150020002500

Note that the wild variance in the Next.js numbers can be explained by the fact that one app avoided lazy-loading images and the other four didn’t. Astro and Vanilla have similar swings that appear to be caused by prioritization or LCP quirks.

In general though, it’s unsurprising that the metric tends to reward MPAs that paint quickly with HTML rather than SPAs that paint after client-side JavaScript runs (along with possibly multiple throttled round-trips to grab the Pokémon data). Ignoring variance, LCP here is mostly a function of JavaScript bundle size. (Qwik is a notable exception here: technically it’s an SPA that uses client-side routing, but it scores among the MPA frameworks.)

Note though that some of the frameworks varied in whether they focused more on the client or the server, or even whether they used a client-side framework. For example, the Gracile agent didn’t even use Lit in two runs. For “Vanilla,” the agent had full latitude (aside from being told to use Vite), but still chose to build an SPA all 5 times.

SSR vs CSR is also partly where the trouble with Angular came from: in 2 runs, the agent built an SSR app that rejected non-localhost (even though the instructions explicitly said that the app would be behind a reverse proxy). I considered this a valid failure to adhere to the spec and decided not to re-run the 2 failed iterations. (This only affects the code size and performance measurements; I have reported all 5 Angular iterations for the “cost” section.)

Maintainability

There are lots of ways to measure maintainability (including fancy things like cyclomatic complexity), but I decided to keep it simple and report something tried-and-true: total lines of code.

Lines of code Framework Hono+htmx 1370 Nuxt 1415 Astro 1461 Vanilla 1492 Next.js 1539 React Router 1564 SvelteKit 1611 SolidStart 1630 TanStack Start 1697 Gracile+Lit 1717 Qwik 1744 Angular 2009 05001000150020002500

To me this is one of the more interesting charts. In a sense, the whole point of a framework is to reduce the amount of code you need to maintain. In Rich Harris’s memorable words:

“Frameworks are not tools for organizing your code; they are tools for organizing your mind.”

– Rich Harris, “Rethinking reactivity”

In the agentic era, this hits even harder because the code size ultimately impacts the number of tokens, including in future edits, meaning it affects the literal cost to maintain a codebase over time. This doesn’t mean that succinctness is the only value that matters, but it’s certainly interesting to see that Hono+htmx can do roughly the same thing as Angular with ~70% of the code (and faster, to boot).

Conclusion

There are many ways you could improve this benchmark. For example, you could mandate that the agent use Service Workers for offline caching, or optimize the Pokémon image files, or use lazy-loading, fetchpriority, the Speculation Rules API, etc. Even though I know a lot of these performance hacks, I deliberately didn’t steer the agents toward any of them, because it’s not what a typical vibe-coder would do.

On the other hand, this entire benchmark could be cheated by just pre-generating all the HTML files as static assets (there are only so many Pokémon). I specifically forebade that in the instructions and made it an explicit check in the test harness, because I felt that it wasn’t in the spirit of the benchmark. (My aim is to simulate a large volume of possibly-dynamic data, which is more challenging than a purely static site.)

You could also improve the way I ran the benchmark by running more iterations, using different coding agents, trying different effort levels, using different frameworks or different versions of the frameworks, trying with and without MCPs/skills, testing in more browsers than just Chromium, building different types of apps, etc. I didn’t do these things mostly in the interest of time. However, if anybody wants to run the benchmark themselves or fork it, it’s on GitHub, so I encourage you to go nuts. I’ll happily report your results here (along with any mistakes or flaws you may find).

My goal here is not to write the end-all-be-all benchmark for “I’m a vibe-coder, which framework should I choose?” The point of this post is to demonstrate that it’s possible in the era of AI coding to still make decisions based on evidence rather than vibes. The benchmark itself is largely vibe-coded, although I did review the code, so if there are mistakes then please consider them mine. I’d also be perfectly happy to see competitor frameworks try to improve on what I’ve done here.

I’m also not trying to vilify any particular framework. I didn’t know which one would “win” before running the benchmark, although I did suspect that MPAs would outperform SPAs (which I’ve cheerfully admitted throughout this post). You could certainly write a more SPA-favored benchmark by making the app a complex dashboard, a video game, a productivity app, etc. You could also pick different metrics: Lighthouse and the Core Web Vitals are pretty tough on SPAs, so you could measure in-app interactivity instead.

I’m also sure that the framework authors themselves could improve their frameworks or AI tools and do better on this benchmark. I have a strong suspicion, for example, that the current crop of MCPs and skills may be doing more harm than good. So if this post is the last word on these frameworks’ performance, I’ll be sorely disappointed. I’m sure there are also emerging frameworks that are champing at the bit to do well on benchmarks such as this one.

If nothing else, I hope this post inspires you to apply additional scrutiny to your choice of JavaScript framework in this weird new era of vibe coding. Are you really picking your tech stack based on evidence? Or are you just going with what you already know? That’s certainly understandable, especially if you’re still reading, reviewing, and debugging the code yourself. But if you’ve gone largely hands-free, then what attachment do you really have to the choices you made back when you were typing code line-by-line like an animal? If you’re re-evaluating the entire way you build software, maybe it’s worth re-evaluating what you type after npm install? Just saying.

Personally, I don’t have any attachment to the frameworks I’ve evaluated above, except that I believe we should strive to build the best possible experiences for our users. I know and respect many of the authors of the above frameworks, and I know that they are working tirelessly for the same values I champion. My hope is just to push the entire community in a better direction toward better, faster, and more accessible frameworks to power the next generation of web apps.

Addendum

Framework versions used in the test (note Qwik had a patch release partway through the test):

Framework Version Angular @angular/core 22.2.3 Astro astro 7.4.2 Gracile+Lit @gracile/gracile 0.11.0, lit 3.3.3 Hono+htmx hono 4.13.14, htmx.org 2.0.11 Next.js next 16.4.3, react 19.3.1 Nuxt nuxt 4.6.2, vue 3.5.44 Qwik @builder.io/qwik-city 1.20.2 (iteration 1), 1.20.3 (iterations 2, 3, 4, 5), @builder.io/qwik 1.20.2 (iteration 1), 1.20.3 (iterations 2, 3, 4, 5) React Router react-router 8.5.0, react 19.3.1 SolidStart @solidjs/start 2.1.0, solid-js 1.9.17 SvelteKit @sveltejs/kit 3.1.0, svelte 5.57.2 TanStack Start @tanstack/react-start 1.169.4, react 19.3.1 Vanilla vite 8.3.5
