entry.title: Domain hacks with unusual Unicode characters (2018)
entry.content:
Unicode contains a range of symbols which don't get much use. For example, there are separate symbols for TradeMark - ™, Service Mark - ℠, and Prescriptions - ℞.

Nestling among the "Letterlike Symbols" are two curious entries. Both of these are single characters:

Telephone symbol - ℡ Numero Sign - №

What's interesting is both .tel and .no are Top-Level-Domains (TLD) on the Domain Name System (DNS).

So my contact site - https://edent.tel/ - can be written as - https://edent.℡/

And the Norwegian domain name registry NORID can be accessed at https://www.norid.№/

Copy and paste those links - they work in any browser!

Is this limited to TLDs?

No! This works ANYWHERE in a domain name. Copy and paste these examples:

Script https://ℰ𝒳𝒜ℳ𝓟ℒℰ.𝒞𝓞ℳ/ Math Bold https://𝐞𝐱𝐚𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞.𝐜𝐨𝐦/ Fraktur https://𝖊𝖝𝖆𝖒𝖕𝖑𝖊.𝖈𝖔𝖒/ Math bold italic https://𝒆𝒙𝒂𝒎𝒑𝒍𝒆.𝒄𝒐𝒎/ Math bold script https://𝓮𝔁𝓪𝓶𝓹𝓵𝓮.𝓬𝓸𝓶/ Double struck https://𝕖𝕩𝕒𝕞𝕡𝕝𝕖.𝕔𝕠𝕞/ Monospace https://𝚎𝚡𝚊𝚖𝚙𝚕𝚎.𝚌𝚘𝚖/ Super script https://ᵉˣᵃᵐᵖˡᵉ.ᶜᵒᵐ/ Sub script https://ₑₓₐₘₚₗₑ.cₒₘ/ NB not all characters supported Math sans bold https://𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲.𝗰𝗼𝗺/ Math sans bold italic https://𝙚𝙭𝙖𝙢𝙥𝙡𝙚.𝙘𝙤𝙢/ Math sans italic https://𝘦𝘹𝘢𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘦.𝘤𝘰𝘮/ Math Squared https://🄴🅇🄰🄼🄿🄻🄴.🄲🄾🄼/ NB the dot must not be squared Circled https://ⓔⓧⓐⓜⓟⓛⓔ.ⓒⓞⓜ/ NB the dot must not be circled

There are a whole bunch more miscellaneous characters you can use:

 How does this work?

Magic! Which is to say, I think it is the browser doing the conversion. DNS Servers don't successfully reply to queries about .℡ domains.

The browser sees the .℡ and then follows the IDNA2008 process listed in RFC5895 to normalise it:

map characters to the "Simple_Lowercase_Mapping" property (the fourteenth column) in <http://www.unicode.org/Public/UNIDATA/UnicodeData.txt>, if any.

The ℡ entry is:

2121;TELEPHONE SIGN;So;0;ON;<compat> 0054 0045 004C;;;;N;T E L SYMBOL;;;;

U+0054 is T, U+0045 is E, U+004C is L.

You can test this in Python using:

python -c 'import sys;print sys.argv[1].decode("utf-8").encode("idna")' "℡" Does this work?

Yes! I asked people on Twitter whether they could access my website using a .℡ - and it appeared to work on every modern browser and operating system.

It even works on command line tools like wget and curl.

It does fail in some circumstances:

 What are the limitations?

Two main ones:

Sites like Twitter and Facebook don't recognise it as a valid URl and refuse to auto link it. Some command line tools like dig and host don't understand it Bashdig edent.℡ ; <<>> DiG 9.10.6 <<>> edent.℡ ;; global options: +cmd ;; Got answer: ;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NXDOMAIN, id: 55282 Is this useful?

Obviously yes. This may be the most important discovery of the decade. You get cool looking URls and get to save a couple of characters on specific domains, at the minor expense of working inconsistently.

It could also be used for evading URl filters.

Every modern browser supports these "fancy" domain names - but most websites won't automatically link to them. So sharing on Facebook doesn't work.

Where can it be used?

Here are the single characters which can be normalised down to a valid TLD. They're mostly country codes, but there are a few interesting exceptions:

㏕ - US Military ℡ - .tel registry № - Norway ㍳ - Australia ㍷ - Dominica ㎀ - Panama ㎁ - Namibia ㎃ - Morocco ㎊ - French Polynesia ㎋ - Norfolk Island ㎏ - Kyrgyzstan ㎖ - Mali ㎙ - Federated States of Micronesia ﬁ - Finland ㎜ - Myanmar ㎝ - Cameroon ㎞ & ㏎ - Comoros ㎰ - Palestine ㎳ - Montserrat ㎷ & ㎹ - Republic of Maldives. ㎺ - Palau ㎽ & ㎿ - Malawi ㏄ - Cocos (Keeling) Islands ㏅ - Democratic Republic of Congo ㏉ - Guyana ㏗ - Philippines ㏘ - Saint Pierre and Miquelon ㏚ - Puerto Rico ㏛ - Suriname ㏜ - El Salvador ℠ - San Marino ™ - Turkmenistan ﬆ & ﬅ - São Tomé and Príncipe ㎇ - Great Britain ( Obsolete) ß - South Sudan ( Not available) ㏌ - India and Indiana (subdomain of .us) Ⅵ & ⅵ - Virgin Islands and Virginia (subdomain of .us) ﬂ - Florida (subdomain of .us) ㎚ - New Mexico (subdomain of .us) ㎵ - Nevada (subdomain of .us) ㍵ - As part of .ovh

If you can find any more, please stick a comment in the box below.

You can always reach this blog post at:

https://🅂𝖍𝐤ₛᵖ𝒓.ⓜ𝕠𝒃𝓲/🆆🆃🅵/

entry.title: Show HN: OmniDiff – Opensource, super fast, content aware Git difftool, in Rust
entry.content:
Fast, robust, accurate content-aware diffing.

Robust: can diff 99.95% of code changes Content-aware: 98.8% of changes diffed using content-specific algorithms Content Fast: under 100ms Accurate: perfect Accurate: near-perfect Code 98% 70% 92% Pictures 96% 69% 91% Cursors 100% 85% 100% Fonts 95% 82% 100% Archives 88% 87% 87% Message catalogs 100% 83% 83% PDFs 57% 100% 100%

Speed measured on a T14s, Intel Core i7-1370P with 32 GB RAM (see Fast). PDFs have fewer than ten judged test cases (see Accurate).

See it in the browser: twenty real code changes, recorded from the command-line tool and compared side by side in Unix diff and in OmniDiff, and content examples: an OpenDocument file, a compiled translation catalog, and pictures, still and animated.

Various light and dark themes are available:

Files are diffed based on type. A PDF diagram with one box renamed, and a web font with twenty icons redrawn:

cargo install --locked omnidiff

This command builds OmniDiff from source, with the dependency versions it was tested with. You need a C compiler on PATH and a Rust toolchain, rustc 1.92 or later. The build compiles every tree-sitter grammar from C. The first cargo install takes a few minutes, because of this and the lto = "fat" release profile.

Prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon), and Windows are attached to every GitHub release.

macOS and Linux:

brew install ivankovic/omnidiff/omnidiff

.deb packages for amd64 and arm64 are available in a signed apt repository:

sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings curl -fsSL https://ivankovic.github.io/omnidiff/apt/omnidiff-archive-keyring.gpg \ | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/omnidiff-archive-keyring.gpg > /dev/null echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/omnidiff-archive-keyring.gpg] \ https://ivankovic.github.io/omnidiff/apt stable main" \ | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/omnidiff.list > /dev/null sudo apt update && sudo apt install omnidiff

On NixOS, or anywhere with Nix installed:

nix run github:ivankovic/omnidiff

If flakes are not enabled in your Nix configuration, add --extra-experimental-features 'nix-command flakes' after nix.

Recipes for Arch and Gentoo live in packaging/: the PKGBUILD builds locally with makepkg -si, and the Gentoo ebuild is ready for an overlay. The two distros are overwhelmed and their repositories open and close to new packages sporadically.

VS Code does not yet let an extension replace its built-in diff view. The API is implemented upstream but unreleased; the extension will adopt it when it ships.

VS Code - omnidiff-vscode. Search for OmniDiff in the Extensions view, or code --install-extension ivankovic.omnidiff. Also on Open VSX for VSCodium, Cursor and Windsurf. Neovim - omnidiff.nvim. omnidiff # open an empty viewer; press o to pick each file omnidiff BEFORE AFTER # open directly into the diff of two files

Press ? in the viewer for the full list of keybindings.

The TUI uses 24-bit color when the terminal advertises it with COLORTERM=truecolor, and the nearest 256 colors otherwise (macOS Terminal.app, or most terminals over ssh, which does not forward COLORTERM). If your terminal supports 24-bit color but does not advertise it, run export COLORTERM=truecolor.

For reviewing changes in a browser, see codereview.

Note: codereview is at v0.0.0; use it at your own risk.

omnidiff --headless BEFORE AFTER, or its synonym --batch, prints the diff as plain text, with optional color, instead of opening the TUI. Use this for scripts or CI. Headless mode also starts automatically whenever stdout is not a terminal, for example when piped into less or redirected to a file. Because of this, omnidiff BEFORE AFTER | less works without the flag.

OmniDiff collapses long runs of unchanged lines. It keeps 3 lines of context on each side of a change (override with --context N), the same convention as diff -u. OmniDiff also prefixes each hunk with the nearest enclosing function, class, or struct line, when that line is not otherwise visible. This shows the location of a change deep inside a large file.

Colors are on by default; pass --color never, or set NO_COLOR=1, to disable ANSI colors, for example when you redirect output to a file - --color always forces them even under NO_COLOR.

OmniDiff exits 0 on success and 2 on error. For scripting, pass --exit-code to additionally get 1 when the files differ. This follows the diff(1) convention. --exit-code is opt-in rather than the default for the same reason git diff exits 0 even when files differ: OmniDiff's usual non-interactive callers are version control systems driving it as a display tool, and they read a non-zero exit as "the tool failed" - jj warns on every file, and git difftool with difftool.trustExitCode=true aborts the whole diff. (The 7-argument GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF form stays at 0 even with --exit-code, since git treats a non-zero exit there as fatal.)

omnidiff --mode json BEFORE AFTER prints the diff as one JSON object. Its fields are described in src/tui/json_output.schema.json, a JSON Schema.

OmniDiff is a git difftool backend. Run the interactive setup wizard, which asks whether to configure it globally or for the current repository only:

omnidiff git configure git config difftool.omnidiff.cmd 'omnidiff "$LOCAL" "$REMOTE"' git difftool --tool=omnidiff

Run git config diff.tool omnidiff to make plain git difftool use OmniDiff by default, without needing --tool. If you do not want git to ask "view diff ... [Y/n]?" before every file, run git config difftool.prompt false.

git difftool opens the interactive TUI. git diff and git log -p never do. git diff pipes its output through git's pager, and a full-screen TUI cannot draw onto a pipe, so OmniDiff always falls back to plain text there regardless of terminal or GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF config (see "Headless / batch mode" above). If you want the interactive viewer from git, use git difftool, not git diff. If git difftool still doesn't open interactively over SSH, reconnect with ssh -t — the session needs an allocated pseudo-terminal; tmux panes always have one.

OmniDiff also works directly with git diff and git log -p, through GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF. This path needs no difftool config:

GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF=omnidiff git diff

Pictures, archives, fonts and the rest of the supported content get a short report of what changed in them. Any other binary file gets a one-line Binary file <path> differs notice instead of a diff, the same stand-in git and diff(1) print for them. Neither ever blocks the rest of a git diff: an external diff that exits non-zero makes git abandon the entire run, so OmniDiff reports an unshowable file as a successful diff of nothing rather than as a failure.

jj does not read git's difftool/diff.external settings, even in a colocated repo, so it needs its own configuration. Run the setup wizard:

omnidiff jj configure jj config set --user merge-tools.omnidiff.program omnidiff jj config set --user merge-tools.omnidiff.diff-args '["$left","$right"]' jj config set --user merge-tools.omnidiff.diff-invocation-mode file-by-file

That registers jj diff --tool omnidiff. To make it the default for plain jj diff as well:

jj config set --user ui.diff-formatter omnidiff

Use --repo in place of --user to configure the current repository only.

diff-invocation-mode = "file-by-file" is required. jj's default hands a diff tool two directory trees; OmniDiff diffs two files, so without this setting every invocation fails. With it, jj passes one changed file pair at a time, keeping each file's real path and extension, so language detection works exactly as it does under git.

jj diff runs its formatter under a pager, so OmniDiff renders in its non-interactive text mode there - the same output git diff gets. jj has no equivalent of git difftool's interactive per-file viewer (its terminal-attached hook, ui.diff-editor, is for jj diffedit/jj split, which edit the right-hand side and read it back - not something a read-only viewer should claim to do), so for the full-screen TUI on a jj repo, run omnidiff BEFORE AFTER directly.

The language is detected from the file extension. A file with an unknown extension is diffed as plain text, line by line, so nothing is refused.

25 languages are parsed with a tree-sitter grammar and diffed structurally:

Language File extensions C .c, .h C# .cs C++ .cc, .cpp, .cxx, .hpp, .hh, .hxx CSS .css, .scss Go .go HTML .html, .htm Java .java JavaScript .js, .mjs, .cjs, .jsx JSON .json Kotlin .kt Lua .lua Perl .pl, .pm PHP .php Python .py, .pyi, .pyw R .r Ruby .rb Rust .rs Scala .scala Shell (Bash) .bash, .sh Swift .swift TSX .tsx TypeScript .ts, .mts, .cts Vimscript .vim XML .xml, .xht, .xhtml, .svg, .glif, .plist, .ui, .qrc, .glade, .xib, .storyboard, .xaml, .vcxproj, .filters, .csproj, .fsproj, .vbproj, .props, .targets, .nuspec, .resx, .wxs, .iml, .manifest, .config, .policy, .xsd, .xsl, .xslt, .xlf, .xliff, .kml, .gpx, .rss, .atom, .graphml, .dae YAML .yaml, .yml

Recognised by extension but diffed as plain text, since no grammar is compiled in: Bazel (.bazel), Dart (.dart), Emacs Lisp (.el), Markdown (.md, .markdown), Protocol Buffers (.proto), SQL (.sql).

Files that are not text are recognised by their bytes, never by their names, and diffed by what they hold:

Content Formats Diffed Pictures PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, ICO, TIFF pixel by pixel, as the eye compares them: how much changed and where; animations frame by frame Archives zip (and so jar, Office documents, EPUB), tar, gzip, xz, bzip2 file by file, each by what it is, archives inside archives included; Java class files as a listing of their fields and methods Fonts TrueType, OpenType, WOFF, WOFF2, EOT glyph by glyph, each drawn, and the font's names and metrics Cursors Windows .cur and .ani, X cursors, Hyprland .hlc size by size and frame by frame Message catalogs gettext .mo, Qt .qm message by message Documents page by page, each page drawn Text in other encodings UTF-16 and UTF-32 with a byte order mark as text, like any other file

Only the members that changed are opened, so a font with two edited glyphs shows two glyphs. Each change is also named by how much of it a reader would see: invisible (only the bytes differ), imperceptible, artifacts (what compression or resampling leaves behind), edited, redrawn or replaced - for text, whitespace, formatting and rewritten stand in for the second, third and fifth.

The TUI shows pictures as pictures: in the terminal's own graphics where it speaks the kitty, sixel or iTerm2 protocol, and in Unicode half blocks everywhere else. b switches to half blocks and back, and OMNIDIFF_GRAPHICS=halfblocks (or kitty, sixel, iterm2) overrides the detection; inside tmux, the terminal in front of the pane decides. An archive, a font or any other container lists its changed members beside the one selected, g shows every changed glyph or picture at once, and Enter opens a text member in the full diff view.

Anything else binary gets the one-line Binary file <path> differs notice.

See the LICENSE file for the full text of the License.

The terms are in LICENSE-COMMERCIAL. Pick the tier that names the commercial license as a benefit. For invoicing or other arrangements, contact me at marko@ivankovic.me.

OmniDiff's goal is:

A median diff in 100ms or less. A 99th-percentile diff in 1000ms or less.

Both are met. Over the 2,302 fixtures in src/test/data/diffs/, measured 2026-10-31 on a laptop, an Intel Core i7-1370P (6 performance and 8 efficiency cores, 20 threads) with 32 GB RAM: p50 4.2ms, p90 35.1ms, p99 177ms, slowest 482ms. 100ms is the 97.6th percentile — 55 fixtures take longer than that, and none takes longer than a second.

Times belong to the machine that measured them, so each machine keeps its own (see research/data/machines.csv): the Intel Xeon E3-1275 v5 server that measured the research figures takes about 2.5 times as long per fixture. Runtime is reported, never gated: make check-quality prints this distribution against the machine's own committed baseline on every push, and warns when the runtime is more than twice the baseline's.

Other content is timed over pairs sampled from the same corpus, decoding included - unpacking an archive, drawing a font's glyphs or a PDF's pages - measured 2026-10-17 on the same laptop:

Content Pairs p50 p90 p99 Under 100ms Pictures 230 1.8ms 41ms 526ms 96.1% Cursors 22 0.6ms 1.3ms 15ms 100% Fonts 100 6.4ms 57ms 826ms 95% Archives 100 2.6ms 156ms 1,938ms 88% Message catalogs 81 0.4ms 1.9ms 4.7ms 100% PDFs 100 69ms 310ms 985ms 57%

Archives miss the 99th-percentile goal: the slowest hold thousands of changed members. PDFs meet both goals, but only 57% of them take under 100ms, since a PDF draws every changed page. make benchmark-content measures this and writes research/data/performance/content_speed/<machine>.csv.

OmniDiff's goal is to process 100% of all commits.

The full test dataset holds the git commit history of about 7,500 open-source git repositories, as available on the main branch. This list of repositories comes from the Gentoo Linux distribution. Find it in list_of_repositories.csv.

Measured over every modified code file in the most recent 50 commits of each of those repositories - 442,530 readable before/after pairs in 25 languages, diffed with no size cap under a 120-second budget and a 6 GB memory cap per process - 442,322 (99.95%) completed successfully. 96 pairs ran past the budget and 112 past the memory cap; the latter are twenty files, nineteen of them generated or embedded - tree-sitter parser tables, codegen, minified bundles, a PNG as a C array - and one commit of a 40,000-line single-header C++ library. Given 24 GB and 300 s, 11 of the 28 files that first hit the cap complete. The run, its harness and every pair that did not complete are documented in research/data/performance/PROVENANCE.md.

Beyond code, over every file changed in the same window - 2,018,010 changes in 7,352 repositories, pictures, fonts and archives included - 98.8% are diffed as text or by their content (98.2% counting each repository at most 1,000 times, so that a few giant ones do not decide it; 6,481 repositories entirely). What is left is mostly text in legacy encodings, compiled objects, audio, and EOT fonts compressed with MicroType Express. The census is documented in research/data/corpus_stats/PROVENANCE.md.

OmniDiff must match a human's own reading of a change, measured against the hand-authored ground-truth mappings in src/test/data/diffs/:

90% of test cases with zero mismatched bytes. 99% of test cases with at most 1% of bytes mismatched.

Neither is met yet. 1,419 of the 2,302 fixtures carry a hand-painted ground truth - every byte of both files labelled with what a human says happened to it - and OmniDiff's own highlighting is compared against it byte by byte, under each of its two highlighting presets (--full, which keeps brackets, separators and leading whitespace, and --minimal, which drops them):

preset zero mismatched bytes at most 1% mismatched mismatched bytes, whole corpus --full 851 (60.0%) 1,241 (87.5%) 99,157 of 73.3M (0.14%) --minimal 987 (69.6%) 1,299 (91.5%) 51,740 of 73.3M (0.07%)

The whole-corpus rate is far below 1% because most of each file is unchanged and nobody gets that wrong; the per-test-case numbers are the ones that count, since a reader meets the mistakes one diff at a time. Most of what is left is not in the matching: rendering the human's own node mapping still disagrees with the painting on 91% of the --full bytes and 91% of the --minimal ones, so the highlighting rules own the gap more than the matcher does.

make update-painting-attribution measures this and writes one row per fixture and preset to research/data/quality/painting_attribution.csv, which the table is counted from; make check-painting-attribution fails if any fixture gets worse.

Other content is judged rather than painted: a human names how much each change is (invisible, imperceptible, artifacts, edited, redrawn or replaced, see supported content) and OmniDiff's verdict is compared with theirs. A test case is perfect when every verdict matches, and near-perfect when every one is at most one level off:

Content Judged Perfect Near-perfect Pictures 130 90 (69%) 118 (91%) Cursors 13 11 (85%) 13 (100%) Fonts 11 9 (82%) 11 (100%) Archives 23 20 (87%) 20 (87%) Message catalogs 12 10 (83%) 10 (83%) PDFs 4 4 (100%) 4 (100%)

make benchmark-content counts these too.

This project uses substantial AI assistance, currently Claude Code. Most commits disclose this with a Co-Authored-By trailer and a link to the session that produced them. This project does not hide that fact. This project does not treat AI assistance as a lesser way to write software.

Contributions are not accepted at this time, to keep the development speed high (see CONTRIBUTING.md). When that changes, AI-assisted contributions will be as welcome as any other, disclosed the same way: whoever submits the work is responsible for understanding it and standing behind it.

See CONTRIBUTING.md for the technology overview, code-quality and testing expectations, project structure, and what CI checks on every push and PR. AGENTS.md has additional AI-agent-specific conventions.

entry.title: Proving and improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs
entry.content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

[Submitted on 29 Oct 2026]

Title:Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAsView PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract:Whether models trained on different modalities converge to the same representation of the world is central to AI. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) conjectures that they do as they scale, but without a proof it offers neither a guarantee nor a recipe. We turn the hypothesis into a theorem. First, we prove a \emph{Platonic Representation Theorem}: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) trained separately on any number of modalities learn the same representation up to one rotation whenever their positive pairs are two observations of one scene--\emph{good views}--and their misalignment is bounded otherwise. Second, we show that next-token prediction is a JEPA with \emph{bad views}, parts of a single document, which explains why language models align with vision only through scale. Third, we validate the theory from 145k captions to the texts of 940M web images, and uncover a scaling law of alignment that predicts unseen runs within seed noise. Good views need 42 times fewer training samples than next-token prediction on the same corpus to reach the same alignment, and a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with DINOv2 and CLIP's image encoders better than every language model we evaluated, up to 72B parameters, and than CLIP's text encoder: next-token prediction is a remarkably inefficient route to platonic representations. As a showcase, one rotation turns separately trained encoders into an image captioner (CIDEr .838 on COCO). Even that rotation needs no pair: on the latest pair-free benchmark, our text JEPA beats every zero-shot accuracy reported with language models up to 8B parameters, e.g., 64\% against at most 56\% top-5 on ImageNet-100. Positive views, and not scale alone, are thus the lever to build platonic representations. Submission historyFrom: Randall Balestriero [view email]

entry.title: Novellas with Groff
entry.content:
blog - git - desktop - contact

2026-10-31

I recently finished my second "novella".

Don't even think about it: I won't publish this. Nor send it to you privately, which is mostly the same as publishing it.

The first story is roughly 50 A5 pages long (~15k words), the second one is about 120 pages (~40k words). (Both barely fit the definition of a "novella", apparently, with the first one being a bit too short and the second one a tiny bit too long.)

It feels pretty absurd and surreal that I have done this at all. In school, anything related to "writing" was pure horror for me -- unless it was related to maths, physics, or other "technical" stuff. But here we are.

How long did it take? Well, the first one took over seven months. But the second one, the longer one? Ten days.

Some time last year, probably around July, I started reading some of the books that were lying around in my appartment for decades. And this was much more enjoyable than I thought. No idea why. It's not like I never read a book before, but it was always a somewhat boring thing to do and it took me ages -- unless it was something technical. I'm only referring to fiction and novels here. Like, one book per year, tops. Yet, I somehow got hooked last year and now I've read about 30 novels since July 2025. Some faster (a couple of days), some slower (three months).

It wasn't that much of a stretch to try to do this myself.

This blog is still technical in nature, so I'll walk through the software that I used.

Table of contents:

Both of my books (they're not really "books", but I'll keep referring to them as such for the sake of simplicity) are typeset in groff. You know, the thing that usually renders manual pages in your terminal on Linux. groff/troff is a full typesetting system, though, and it can be used to produce real books, which I've already mentioned a couple of times in previous blog posts.

In my case, the appeal of groff is that it's relatively small and fast, but still able to produce high-quality output. Making that 50-page document takes about 700 ms on my 13.5 year old PC, and the 120-page one takes 1.6 seconds. This includes some pre-processing which we'll cover later. Given that most modern software these days feels like walking in mud, this is refreshingly quick.

Because it's more fun that way, I made my own little macro package. There really isn't a lot to it, though. It's tiny. Not a lot is needed for a simple novel / novella -- no table of contents, no cross-references, no diagrams, no code blocks, no lists, ... Just nicely flowing text and sometimes a word gets emphasized.

Disclaimer: You'll note some TODO items in the text below. groff is a full-blown typesetting system and these things are complicated. I'm a long way from having mastered every aspect of it.

There are only three macros:

.\" Section header / chapter title .de SH . sp 1v . ps +5p . ce \f[HR]\\$1\fP . ps . sp 4v .. .\" Normal paragraph with hanging indent. .de PP . br . ti +2m .. .\" "Long" paragraph, longer empty space. .de LP . sp 2v ..

(The name SH is a spill-over from manual pages. I've written quite a few of those and this name somehow stuck. CH for "chapter heading" or CT for "chapter title" might have been better choices. Or, you know, .CHAPTER.)

You start defining a macro with .de -- anything until .. is part of that macro.

.SH: Go down one vee, increase type size, request centering, print the macro's first argument with the HR font (Helvetica), return to previous type size, add another four vees of space..PP: Just break the current line, then request a temporary indent for the next output line. This creates a hanging indent, which is customary in German books..LP: Just some empty space between paragraphs. Used for things like intra-chapter time jumps.

You can look up the individual commands in man 7 groff.

And that would already be enough to produce a document that somewhat resembles a book.

Put the snippet above in a file called macros.groff. I made one file per chapter. For example: chapter01.groff. You can then make a PDF using a command like this:

groff -Tpdf -dpaper=a5 -P-pa5 macros.groff chapter01.groff >book.pdf

A5 is roughly the page size of a "typical book".

You'll note that there are no page numbers by default. You could actually just decide to not have them if all you want is a digital PDF. They're useful for printing, but you don't really need them in a file, if we're being honest.

Except: The thing gets confused about page breaks. Create the PDF using the example above and you'll see:

Looks like the baseline of the last line of output is just outside the page. Not sure what's going on here -- it's related to setting the page size to A5. In other words, I probably missed another spot where this has to be set. It'll be fixed implicitly by the following.

The whole page number thing consists of three parts: First, how large is the footer (the area where the page numbers live)? I defined this in a register (which is not really necessary but I find the "code" easier to read this way) -- the name is arbitary:

.nr _FooterSize 5v

We than plant a trap at the bottom of the page:

.wh -\n[_FooterSize]u _FooterTrap

\n[_FooterSize] "gets" the value of the register called _FooterSize. There's a minus sign in front of it, it's negative and relative to the bottom of the page. The documentation says:

A general-purpose register (one created or updated with the nr request) is implicitly dimensionless, or reckoned in basic units if interpreted in a measurement context.

I'm not 100% sure why I need to add the u. I haven't read every page of the manual, yet. Needless to say, it doesn't work without it.

Okay, so the trap gets installed at 5v before the end of the page and it'll call the _FooterTrap macro. It looks like this:

.de _FooterTrap .\" Push current environment on stack and switch to `_FooterEnv`. .\" Parent env will keep partially collected lines. . ev _FooterEnv .\" Copy settings from default environment. . evc 0 .\" Don't do this for pages 1 and 2, they're title pages in my actual .\" "book". . if \\n[%]>2 \{\ .\" Set vertical position, explained in the text below. . sp |\\n[.p]u-2v .\" Print % register centered. . ce \fR\\n[%]\fP \} .\" Go back to previous environment. . ev .\" Request page break. ' bp ..

It's much easier to read without the inline comments:

.de _FooterTrap . ev _FooterEnv . evc 0 . if \\n[%]>2 \{\ . sp |\\n[.p]u-2v . ce \fR\\n[%]\fP \} . ev ' bp ..

Why is it 'bp instead of .bp? We'll get to that.

What I'm unsure about: I set the vertical position to |\\n[.p]u-2v. That's relative to the top of the page, it's the page length minus two vee. I would have expected |-2v-1v (including the "minus one vee" mentioned in the docs) to also work, but that leads to an infinite loop (probably triggers the same trap again and again). Why?

For symmetry, I also want some empty space at the top of the page:

.nr _HeaderSize 5v .de _HeaderTrap ' sp |\\n[_HeaderSize]u .. .wh 0v _HeaderTrap

And another TODO for me: This isn't 100% symmetrical. The length of the header is a bit larger than the footer. An issue with the page size again?

Let's have a closer look at traps. I'm not 100% sure on this -- this is to the best of my understanding.

Actually, let's take a step back from the example above. Let's start with this:

This is a little excerpt from Mary Shelly's Frankenstein. These visions faded when I perused, for the first time, those poets whose effusions entranced my soul and lifted it to heaven. I also became a poet and for one year lived in a paradise of my own creation; I imagined that I also might obtain a niche in the temple where the names of Homer and Shakespeare are consecrated. You are well acquainted with my failure and how heavily I bore the disappointment. But just at that time I inherited the fortune of my cousin, and my thoughts were turned into the channel of their earlier bent. Six years have passed since I resolved on my present undertaking. I can, even now, remember the hour from which I dedicated myself to this great enterprise. I commenced by inuring my body to hardship. I accompanied the whale-fishers on several expeditions to the North Sea; I voluntarily endured cold, famine, thirst, and want of sleep; I often worked harder than the common sailors during the day and devoted my nights to the study of mathematics, the theory of medicine, and those branches of physical science from which a naval adventurer might derive the greatest practical advantage. Twice I actually hired myself as an under-mate in a Greenland whaler, and acquitted myself to admiration. I must own I felt a little proud when my captain offered me the second dignity in the vessel and entreated me to remain with the greatest earnestness, so valuable did he consider my services.

Save it as test.groff and make a PDF:

groff -Tpdf test.groff >book.pdf

Looks like this:

Install a trap at 10v. It's empty so far and does nothing -- insert this at the very top of the file:

.de MyTrap .. .wh 10v MyTrap .\"

The PDF looks the same.

Now what happens when we change the trap macro to this?

.de MyTrap FOO ..

This is the result:

When the output reached the word "fishers", it sprang the trap. "FOO" comes after "fishers" in the PDF: "fishers" triggered the trap, then "FOO" got inserted. I think it's as simple as that, isn't it?

Suppose we want to put "FOO" at the beginning of the line and we want nothing but that word on that line. "fishers" shall be put on the next line.

If I understand correctly, switching environments is key: The environment holds the currently collected line (among many other things). Switch to a new one and we get a new buffer/line -- one that's empty so far. We can then flush/break this line to have it included in the PDF, and then switch back to the previous environment:

.de MyTrap . ev MyTrapEnv FOO . br . ev ..

So far, so good. Now I want there to be an empty line before and after "FOO":

.de MyTrap . ev MyTrapEnv . sp FOO . sp . ev ..

In the new environment, we issue .sp: It breaks and inserts space. Nothing was collected so far, so the break doesn't print anything at this point. Then we have FOO -- this isn't printed directly, it's just collected. The next .sp breaks again (thus printing "FOO") and then inserts more space.

Okay. Now. Suppose that printing "FOO" with those two lines around it is all we want to do inside of the trap. We then want the normal text to continue at some absolute position on the page, say at 17v.

So, how about the following? We go back to the previous environment and then issue an absolute location request:

.de MyTrap . ev MyTrapEnv . sp FOO . sp . ev . sp |17v ..

Oops:

.sp |17v broke the already collected line (the one with just "fishers" in it) and then inserted the space. We don't want that break. (Also note that "fishers" is at the exact same position where we left off inside the trap.)

This can be avoided by using ' instead of .:

' The neutral apostrophe is the no-break control character, recâ ognized where the control character is. It suppresses the (first) break implied by the bp, ce, cf, fi, fl, "in", nf, rj, sp, ti, and trf requests. The requested operation takes efâ fect at the next break.

So let's do this:

.de MyTrap . ev MyTrapEnv . sp FOO . sp . ev ' sp |17v ..

Result:

The example in the documentation doesn't change environments. But I find it much easier to understand what's going when changing them. (And I hope I got it right.)

One final remark: Environment carry settings. .ev foo starts a completely new environment (unless an environment with that name already exists), it doesn't clone the previous one. That's why my macro package also does .evc 0.

As a little exercise, see what happens when you use 'sp |12v, 'sp |11.5v, 'sp |11v, all the way down to 'sp |9v.

Only when writing this blog post, I found the following sentence in the docs (Basics):

If you don't start a sentence on a new line, put two spaces after the previous sentence. GNU troff then recognizes punctuation that ends a sentence, and inserts inter-sentence space accordingly.

I didn't do that, because this isn't customary in German. But now I see it. Sometimes, it looks like this in the PDF:

Foo. Bar.

And sometimes there's a little bit of extra space:

As far as I know, this is usually not done in German books. I disabled it with this request, which keeps "minimal inter-word spacing" at the default value of 12 but sets "supplemental inter-sentence spacing" to 0:

.ss 12 0

This isn't part of my macro package, but it comes first in the "index" file (book.groff, see demo package below).

Apparently, it's as simple as this:

.hla den .hpf hyphen.den

den is "de(utsch) new": This includes the "new" German rules from 2006.

I actually wrote both of my stories in plain groff, using the macros I explained above.

Markdown has the big advantage of being "visually pleasing": It mostly looks like text that is intended to be read by a human being. groff isn't, really. I mean, it wasn't horrible, I wouldn't have written over 170 pages in groff if this was pain. It's fine. I use groff in several other places as well. But Markdown is a tiny little bit better, and I assume that it allows me to focus more on the creative process.

So, afterwards, I converted the second story to "Markdown". Didn't bother to do that for the first one. I put that in quotation marks because there are only very few elements, it's not full Markdown:

# Chapter title at the top of the file.--- for "long empty paragraphs".*foo* for emphasized text.

And that's it. Makes the conversion really easy.

I could have just use plain Markdown for this whole thing and created an HTML file. I already have the tooling for that -- that's what drives my blog. Maybe this could even produce a PDF file. But what would be missing there, among other things, would be an engine to properly justify text. It hurts my eyes to see justified text in HTML, it just looks like a complete disaster. The results that groff or TeX create are much, much better.

While we're at it, we can also do some basic character replacements: I have the German typographic quotation marks U+201E and U+201C directly on my keyboard, but Guillemets are preferred in books.

I first wanted to do all this in Python but then switched to a little Perl snippet, because it makes it easy to read the entire file and then do multiline-regex stuff on it. It goes something like this:

perl -0pe ' # Guillemets are preferred in books. s/... German typographic quotes, see demo package .../... Guillemets .../g; # Markdown "h1" into ".SH". s/^# ([^\n]+)\n/.SH "\1"\n/smg; # Markdown "hr" into ".LP". s/\n---\n/.LP/smg; # Markdown paragraphs into ".PP". s/\n\n/\n.PP\n/smg; # Markdown emphasize into groff font selection: s/\*([^*]+)\*/\\fI\1\\fP/smg; '

The output is still groff for my little macro package. But I can now write it like this:

# Kapitel 42: Die Antwort Da war sie also. Die Antwort auf *alle* Fragen. Und dann ging es weiter: Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit. Vestibulum hendrerit blandit suscipit. Maecenas sed nisi nec ante mattis vulputate. Pellentesque maximus leo id purus vestibulum dictum. Donec tincidunt mollis viverra. Curabitur at ligula in turpis pellentesque vehicula. Duis hendrerit commodo mauris, non posuere leo vulputate ut. Nulla finibus urna eget vehicula auctor. Mauris in posuere nibh. Vivamus ut metus vel nisi gravida molestie vitae et tellus. Integer mi odio, vestibulum eget laoreet vel, auctor nec ligula. Quisque eu placerat quam, eu tincidunt mauris. Nam vestibulum lectus non leo dignissim, non sagittis dolor venenatis.

This reads much nicer and there is syntax highlighting in Vim for it. Well, the *emphasized* parts, that is -- the rest doesn't matter:

Speaking of Vim ...

There is one super important Vim plugin for this:

https://github.com/junegunn/goyo.vim

It hides almost all UI elements.

On top of that, I put the terminal window in fullscreen mode to hide my desktop.

And there you go. "Distraction-free writing" indeed. Maybe put on some music, but there's nothing else. No browser, no clock, no nothing. Just a typewriter with an easy undo function.

The font is the 11x22 variant of UW ttyp0.

There's a popular way to format text in plain-text files:

This is one sentence. This is another one. And so on and so on. One sentence per line, that's it. Sentences can be short. Or they can be pretty long, sometimes even exceeding the available width on your screen, thus requiring you to either scroll or have your editor soft-wrap it for you when displaying it.

As we've learned above from the groff docs, this actually carries meaning for groff (properly detect the ends of sentences). And it makes the diffs in VCS's less noisy.

Another popular way would be to put each paragraph on its own line. Like, there's only one "physical" newline character after the whole thing and it's your editor's job to properly display this:

I used the second version for a couple of years at the end of the 1990ies and the early 2000s, but eventually switched to hard-wrapped text. Like this:

I just find this easier to read and easier to navigate in. And it reminds me of the "good" old DOS days, where I used the T editor a lot and all my files looked like that (manually formatted, of course). It does have drawbacks, yes. It's not great for collaboration with other people, but that doesn't matter in my case.

Another drawback is that I have to reformat these paragraphs while editing. Luckily, Vim makes that easy:

" In ~/.vimrc: set nojs map Q gq}

I can then just put my cursor at the beginning of a paragraph:

[T]his is one sentence. This is another one. And so on and so on. One sentence per line, that's it. Sentences can be short.

And hit Q to turn it into this:

This is one sentence. This is another one. And so on and so on. One sentence per line, that's it. Sentences can be short. [_]

The cursor will be positioned after that paragraph. To reflow the entire document, I can just keep Q pressed down until it hits the end.

-- edit: Or do :set formatoptions+=a to have paragraphs reformatted automatically while editing it. I usually don't want that, I usually want it to be an explicit operation. But for writing prose, this might be pretty useful.

The nojs option (funny name, huh?) was new to me, only found out about it just now. The full name is nojoinspaces and it prevents the very thing that I should be doing (but which is not customary in German): It does not insert two spaces after a period. Without it, i.e., with set js, the result would look like this:

Some people like that, I don't.

As with virtually everything I do, this is in Git.

But that's the end. I regularly commit the current state, but I hardly care about anything else. No proper commit messages, nothing. It's just a tool for making "backups" easier and to sync the data between my laptop and desktop PC.

demo-book.tar.gz: Putting it all together

As I said, I won't publish the actual "books". But here's a demo of the "scaffold":

(I won't update this. This is just a snapshot of the current status.)

I won't say much about this. I'm a total noob.

I changed course a couple of times. For both stories, I tried to draft the whole thing before I began writing the actual text, but that didn't help much. The first story isn't that great anyway. It has an interesting premise, but I wasn't really "in the zone". That's also why it took so long. The second story has a much more mundane basic idea to it and then I eventually realized how interesting it actually was. There are quite a few twists and turns in it, and I love that.

It was way harder than I thought to keep the facts straight, especially with the course changes. Which character knows what, when, why? What are the motives? Is everything consistent and plausible? Constantly question everything -- does she really need to do that now or is there some other, much more likely way out? Does every sentence she said 100 pages ago still make sense after the big reveal at the end? Stuff like that. I'll have to get better at that. Probably use a little "character inventory" next time, like, a profile for each one.

Building a world with its own set of rules and history and what not turns out to be very fascinating. As is building the characters.

The length of the stories make proof-reading ridiculously hard. Like, I'm not going to read 120 pages in a couple of minutes. I re-read the second story one last time yesterday and it took ... *checks notes* ... three hours. Ouch.

Now that I've re-read that 120-page thing again yesterday ... I actually like it. I'm happy with the result. There's obviously a lot to learn: This entire field is completely new to me. I have identified quite a few places where the storytelling isn't great -- the pace isn't right, things progress too fast. (At the moment, I only notice this when reading the whole thing in one go. Oof.) Sometimes the wording isn't great. Not enough detail. And so on. But the story itself is something that I'd enjoy reading myself.

Digging deeper into groff is on my TODO list, also for obvious reasons.

What I really loved about this whole thing is that I ended up completely in the tunnel. On one of those ten days that it took me to write the 120-page thing, I wasn't even actually typing on a keyboard: We were travelling across the country, lots of idle time, I didn't have a laptop, but I basically "wrote" at least one chapter and then memorized (most of) it. Went back and forth, new ideas. Completely absorbed.

I want more of that. :-)

Maybe stuff will eventually get published (as in: I might put it on this website), but not now. I do this for myself. I'm not even remotely interested in my work getting torn apart by rude critics. Leave me alone. :-)

And if you think about suggesting the use of LLMs: Congratulations, you have completely missed the point. "Setzen, 6."

entry.title: Seoul Viosys begins production of rare-earth-free white light emitter
entry.content:
News: LEDs

29 October 2026

Seoul Viosys begins mass production of rare-earth-free white light emitter, with chips as small as 10Âµm

For three decades, white LEDs have depended on rare-earth materials such as yttrium aluminium garnet (YAG) layered onto a blue LED chip (Figure 1). Opto-semiconductor device maker Seoul Viosys Co Ltd (SVC) says that it has now broken that dependence by developing and mass producing a chip that emits white light without rare earths. The chip can be as small as 10Âµm.

Figure 1. New invention: white WICOP 3.

Seoul Viosys and its parent company South Korean LED maker Seoul Semiconductor Co Ltd opened up the micro-LED market with WICOP (Wafer Integrated Chip on PCB), which is a chip architecture that eliminates the package altogether. With WICOP, the two companies have already developed and mass produced ultraviolet, blue, green, red and infrared LEDs smaller than 100Âµm in size. WICOP 3 is the third generation of the technology, extending that capability to white light without rare-earth elements (REEs).

White LED market

White LEDs comprise about $10bn of the $15bn global market for packaged LEDs. WICOP 3 can now replace them with a technology free of rare earths, reckons the firm.

More significantly, WICOP 3 is claimed to be the world’s first white opto-semiconductor to achieve white light in a micro-LED smaller than 100Âµm.

WICOP 3 uses neither rare earths (a major source of environmental pollution) nor a package. Nor does it contain synthetic silicone resins, plastics or lead frames used in conventional LEDs. The result is said to be a far more environmentally friendly product that costs about half as much to make as a conventional white LED.

Creating new markets

The miniaturized transistor replaced the vacuum tube and created vast new markets in electronics. The company believes micro white opto-semiconductors can do the same.

WICOP 3 generates white light from gallium nitride (GaN) alone. Also, the chip contains no plastics, silicone or other synthetic organic materials. It can hence last for decades. In lighting, invisible micro-emitters could be embedded in wallpaper or window glass, lighting a space with no fixtures at all. This would end the inconvenience of replacing bulbs and the high cost of fixtures. The company expects this to create a new market tens of times larger than today's $10bn white LED market.

Performance

In its first mass production, a micro-LED chip measuring just 25Âµm x 10Âµm produced 0.015lm of white light. Its chromaticity falls inside the CIE standard white region (Figure 2). Luminous efficacy is already close to 100lm/W. The company aims to reach 200lm/W within two years. A conventional 1000Âµm x 1000Âµm chip achieves 50lm.

Figure 2. WICOP 3 brightness by size.

Technical significance

Up to now, WICOP could make chips smaller, but white light still required a package containing rare earths. White chips therefore could not go below 1000Âµm. This held back cost reduction. White micro LEDs under 100Âµm (0.1mm) were also out of reach. Removing rare earths changes that. White light is now possible both in large chips of 1000Âµm and above and in micro LEDs below 100Âµm.

Future plans

Seoul Group (consisting of Seoul Semiconductor and Seoul Viosys) will start mass production of WICOP 3 in fourth-quarter 2026. It says it will supply first those customers that have respected its intellectual property and relied on its products.

Seeking supply chain partners

Seoul Viosys uses WICOP to produce micro-emitters smaller than 100Âµm. Micro-LEDs built on WICOP can now carry high volumes of AI data over distances from under 1cm to tens of meters. Over short distances, data has long traveled electrically through copper wire.

Under the data loads of the AI era, copper links slow down, generate heat and consume much more power. Using light instead, Seoul Viosys arranges 1000 WICOP chips of about 10Âµm each in a grid within an area of 1mm2 or less. This array transmits data 10 times faster at one tenth of the power. Market research firms including Omdia forecast that this technology and augmented reality (AR) together will create a new $60bn market within five years (equal to half of today's DRAM memory market).

Seoul Semiconductor’s founder Chung Hoon Lee says that the company intends to target WICOP 1, 2 and 3 at applications in AR glasses and AI data communications. These technologies work on scales of 10Âµm or less. To that end, it is seeking trusted upstream and downstream micro-LED supply chain partners in AR displays and AI transmitters.

Seoul Viosys expanding business beyond components to data-interconnect transceivers
